priorArtifacts.name: Business Model & Financial Projections
priorArtifacts.content:
Bottom-up build basis: This model is built up from the vendor-unit economics established in Checkpoint 14 (R40/month subscription, R14/month COGS, R180 CAC) and the vendor-growth pace implied by our SOM in Checkpoint 3 (targeting ~150 active vendors by month 18), not a top-down revenue target chosen first and reverse-engineered.

INCOME STATEMENT (Year 1):
- Vendor count ramp: 6 (month 1) → 20 (month 3) → 50 (month 6) → 90 (month 9) → 130 (month 12).
- Revenue: R290,000 (vendor-count x R40/month, weighted for ramp).
- COGS: R102,000 (vendor-count x R14/month).
- Gross profit: R188,000 (65% gross margin).
- Operating expenses: R398,000 total — founder drawings R120,000 (R15,000/month from month 5, deferred earlier), technical hire R175,000 (R25,000/month from month 6 for 7 months), USSD gateway platform fee R24,000 (R2,000/month fixed, based on Clickatell's published basic USSD short-code access pricing tier), backup power/connectivity R9,600 (R800/month: a small 500W inverter and deep-cycle battery amortised, plus a 10GB/month mobile data bundle, to keep the founder's laptop, router, and backend dashboard functioning through load-shedding since the customer-facing USSD flow is resilient but the founder's own admin tooling is not), and other admin/travel R69,400.
- EBITDA: -R210,000.

BALANCE SHEET (end of Year 1):
- Cash: R255,000
- Inventory (test-strip stock): R15,000
- Equipment (laptop, basic field kit): R20,000
- Total assets: R290,000
- Liabilities: R0 (no debt)
- Share capital (from the pre-seed raise, Checkpoint 16): R500,000
- Accumulated deficit: -R210,000
- Total equity: R290,000 (balances with total assets)

CASH FLOW STATEMENT (Year 1):
- Operating cash flow: -R210,000 (tracks EBITDA closely; minimal working-capital swings since vendor subscriptions are collected monthly in advance, limiting receivables exposure)
- Investing cash flow: -R35,000 (initial test-strip stock R15,000 + equipment purchase R20,000)
- Financing cash flow: +R500,000 (pre-seed capital raised, per Checkpoint 16)
- Net change in cash: R255,000
- Opening cash (company inception): R0
- Closing cash: R255,000 (matches balance sheet cash position)

Defensible assumptions, stated explicitly: vendor churn is NOT yet modelled with real data (same gap flagged in Checkpoint 14's LTV caveat) — this model assumes zero vendor churn in Year 1, which is optimistic and explicitly flagged rather than hidden; Year 2 planning will require real Year 1 churn data before being credible. The USSD gateway and backup-power line items are sourced from Clickatell's published basic-tier pricing and a standard small-inverter/battery-plus-data-bundle estimate respectively, not unsourced round numbers.

priorArtifacts.name: Legal Entity & Founder Agreements
priorArtifacts.content:
Legal entity status: CIPC name reservation for "Nairobi Tap (Pty) Ltd" was filed and approved (reservation reference obtained via CIPC's online BizPortal, February 2024), and the full company registration (CoR14.1) has been submitted and is pending finalisation — consistent with the 30-60 day timeline disclosed in Checkpoint 7. We are documenting this honestly as in-progress rather than presenting registration as complete before it is, since a founder agreement and IP assignment can be validly executed ahead of formal incorporation and are the higher-priority governance step at this stage.

Founder agreement: A signed founders' agreement is in place between the sole founder (Jane Founder, 100% ordinary shareholding pending registration) and no co-founders at this stage, covering: vesting schedule (4-year vesting, 1-year cliff, standard SAFE-adjacent structure used by South African seed-stage companies), founder responsibilities, and a dedicated IP assignment clause under which all pre-incorporation IP (the USSD verification protocol design, vendor-onboarding methodology, and test-strip sourcing relationships developed to date) is assigned to the company upon incorporation, drafted with reference to standard South African founder-agreement templates used by local accelerators (e.g., the format commonly used by Silicon Cape-affiliated programmes).

Beneficial ownership: Given single-founder ownership at this stage, the beneficial ownership register required under the Companies Act (as amended by the 2023 beneficial ownership amendments implemented in response to FATF grey-listing concerns) will list Jane Founder as 100% beneficial owner at registration. This register is prepared in draft form now so it can be filed within the statutory window immediately upon CIPC registration completing, rather than treated as an afterthought.

IP assignment: Beyond the founders' agreement clause, a standalone IP assignment schedule itemises the specific pre-incorporation assets being assigned: the USSD flow specification document, the vendor onboarding script and training materials developed during the Khayelitsha fieldwork (referenced in Checkpoints 1-2), and the test-strip supplier relationship terms negotiated to date. Itemising these specifically (rather than a blanket "all IP" clause) is intentional, since vague IP assignment clauses are a common diligence flag for South African seed investors.

Gap disclosed honestly: No co-founder or employee IP assignment issues exist yet since there is currently one founder and no employees; this will need to be revisited the moment any contractor or employee is engaged, and is flagged here as a forward-looking governance item rather than deferred silently.

priorArtifacts.name: Demonstrated Traction (type-specific)
priorArtifacts.content:
{"narrative":"Traction context: These figures come from a live pilot run in a single Khayelitsha ward between February and June 2024, using a manual precursor to the full USSD system (a WhatsApp-based number staffed by the founder, standing in for the eventual USSD short-code while telco short-code allocation is finalised, per the regulatory dependency noted in Checkpoint 6).

Signups (148): Defined as unique households who registered by messaging the pilot number to receive vendor safety-check results, verified via unique phone number (no duplicates). Registration was driven entirely through the 6 vendors piloting the tag system, not paid acquisition — each vendor displaying a tag drove organic signups from their existing customer base, which matters because it demonstrates the vendor-distribution logic from Checkpoint 6 actually converts, not just a hypothesis.

MAU (52): Defined as unique households who sent at least one "check vendor status" message in the trailing 30 days (May 2024), verified from the same phone-number log used for signups. This is a genuine active-use metric, not signups reinterpreted — 35% of registered households are actively re-checking monthly, which is the retention signal that matters more than raw signups for a trust-verification product, since the point of the product is repeated use at each purchase decision, not a one-time signup.

Township & income reality check on these numbers: The pilot ward covers roughly 380 households per municipal ward-boundary estimates, so 148 signups represents genuine penetration (~39% of addressable households in that specific micro-area) rather than a vanity number diluted across an unrealistically large denominator — we are reporting the real, narrow base we actually reached, not projecting from a headline settlement-wide population figure that would inflate the apparent traction.

Honest caveat: This is one ward, one settlement, over five months, with a manual (not yet USSD) channel — it validates the demand-side hypothesis (households will register and re-check) but does not yet validate the automated, multi-ward channel this checkpoint's threshold is really testing readiness for. The next milestone (tracked in Checkpoint 18) is converting this manual pilot into the live USSD flow across at least two additional wards.","b2c":{"signups":148,"mau":52}}

priorArtifacts.name: Team Architecture
priorArtifacts.content:
Current team: Jane Founder is currently the sole full-time operator (consistent with the single-founder ownership structure disclosed in Checkpoint 8), covering vendor relationships, fieldwork, and the manual pilot operations described in Checkpoint 11. This is an honest single-founder team at this stage, not a team dressed up to look larger than it is.

Skills present: Township-based field operations and vendor-network management (three years, prior fintech distribution role, Checkpoint 7), direct customer research capability (household and vendor fieldwork conducted personally across Checkpoints 1, 2, 9), and early-stage fundraising/documentation ability (this submission itself).

Gaps, named specifically rather than glossed over: (1) No technical co-founder or engineer — the USSD system described in Checkpoint 4 does not yet exist as working software; it has been scoped but not built, and this is the single largest execution risk to the venture. (2) No public-health or water-quality technical advisor yet formally engaged, though in early conversation (referenced in Checkpoint 7). (3) No finance/operations hire, currently acceptable given the small pilot scale but a near-term need once vendor count grows past roughly 30-40 (the point at which manual reconciliation of test-strip distribution and vendor payments becomes unmanageable for one person, based on comparable informal-distribution ratios the founder observed in the prior fintech role).

Near-term plan to close the largest gap: The technical co-founder/first engineering hire is the top priority for the next quarter, targeted through South African developer networks (e.g., OfferZen, or direct referral from the founder's existing fintech network) rather than an offshore hire, specifically because the USSD integration requires working knowledge of South African telco short-code and USSD gateway providers (e.g., Clickatell, Africa's Talking), which is a local, not generic, technical skill.

Advisory: One informal advisor relationship exists — a former manager from the founder's prior fintech role, providing guidance on vendor-network economics, unpaid and informal at this stage (no equity or formal advisor agreement yet, disclosed honestly rather than presented as a formal advisory board that does not exist).

We are not recruiting a large team prematurely; the plan is deliberately sequenced — technical hire first, then an operations hire once vendor count justifies it, then a formal advisory board once there is a product to advise on, rather than assembling advisors and headcount ahead of proof that the model works.

priorArtifacts.name: Regulatory & Data Compliance
priorArtifacts.content:
POPIA compliance: Building on the beneficial ownership and entity status disclosed in Checkpoint 8, our data model is designed for POPIA minimisation from the outset. The USSD registration flow (Checkpoint 4/11) collects only: phone number, settlement/ward area, and test-result history — explicitly not ID numbers, home addresses, or names, since none of these are required for the core trust-verification function. Consent is captured as an explicit USSD confirmation step at registration ("Reply YES to receive vendor safety alerts"), logged with a timestamp, satisfying POPIA's requirement for a documented lawful basis (consent) rather than relying on an implied-consent argument. A data retention policy (draft) specifies test-result logs older than 12 months are purged rather than retained indefinitely, and a POPIA-compliant privacy notice (in isiXhosa and English, given the primary pilot ward's language profile) is read out via USSD text at registration rather than assuming households will read an emailed policy document they are unlikely to receive or open.

Tax registration: A SARS (South African Revenue Service) income tax reference number will be obtained automatically upon CIPC company registration completing (per Checkpoint 8's registration-in-progress status); VAT registration is not yet required as projected first-year revenue (modelled in Checkpoint 15) falls below the compulsory VAT registration threshold, and voluntary VAT registration is deliberately deferred until revenue is closer to that threshold, to avoid unnecessary compliance overhead at pre-revenue stage.

Sector-specific compliance: Water quality testing sits adjacent to, but is distinct from, formal municipal water supply regulation (the Blue Drop/Green Drop framework applies to municipal and water-service-authority supply, not informal vendor resale, per our review of the Department of Water and Sanitation's published Blue Drop scope documents) — meaning there is no existing formal licensing regime this venture is required to register under for testing informal vendor water, though we are seeking informal confirmation of this reading from the NGO partner referenced in Checkpoint 10 before finalising, rather than assuming a regulatory gap without verifying it.

B-BBEE: As noted in Checkpoint 5, B-BBEE Level 1-2 contributor status will be pursued once turnover crosses the threshold requiring formal verification (Exempt Micro-Enterprise status applies below that threshold, requiring only a sworn affidavit rather than a full verification audit), which is the compliant approach for a company at this revenue stage rather than paying for premature formal B-BBEE verification.

Honest gap: The consent-language localisation (isiXhosa USSD text) is drafted but not yet tested with actual users for comprehension — this is flagged as a pre-launch validation task, not assumed to be correct simply because it has been translated.

priorArtifacts.name: Capital Pathway
priorArtifacts.content:
What's being raised: R500,000 in pre-seed capital, structured as a blend of a small grant component and priced equity rather than pure venture equity, consistent with the SA capital landscape reasoning set out in Checkpoint 5. Specifically: R150,000 targeted from a development-finance or impact-grant source (e.g., an SME/informal-economy support grant of the kind offered by South African DFIs such as the IDC's small enterprise support windows, or municipal enterprise-development programmes tied to informal settlement upgrading), and R350,000 from priced equity via an angel or early-stage impact investor, using a standard SAFE-equivalent instrument common in South African seed rounds (a simple agreement structured similarly to a SAFE, converting at the next priced round).

Why this structure, not pure equity: The grant component reflects that this venture sits within a genuine public-interest/informal-settlement service-delivery gap (Checkpoint 5), which is exactly the kind of activity DFI and municipal enterprise-development grants are designed to support, and taking a portion as non-dilutive capital is more founder- and mission-aligned than taking the full amount as equity when a grant-eligible portion genuinely exists. We are not chasing a full-equity round to appear more "venture-scale" than the business currently is.

Milestone-tied use of funds:
- R180,000 (36%) — first technical hire (per Checkpoint 12), building the live USSD system to replace the manual WhatsApp-based pilot (Checkpoint 11), milestone: functioning USSD flow live in the original pilot ward within 4 months of funding.
- R102,000 (20%) — test-strip inventory and vendor-onboarding operating costs to grow from 6 to 90 vendors (per the Checkpoint 15 ramp), milestone: 90 active vendors and re-validated MAU/retention data (addressing the churn-data gap flagged honestly in Checkpoints 14 and 15) within 9 months.
- R120,000 (24%) — founder drawings once vendor count justifies it, keeping the founder financially sustainable through the raise period rather than assuming unpaid founder labour indefinitely.
- R98,000 (20%) — buffer for the USSD gateway/backup-power opex line items (Checkpoint 15) and a contingency reserve, given this is the first raise and unforeseen costs (e.g., telco short-code delays, per the regulatory risk noted in Checkpoint 6) are realistic.

Capital pathway sequencing: This pre-seed round is explicitly sized to fund the milestones needed to raise a larger, priced seed round (targeting the 90-vendor, validated-retention milestone as the proof point for that next raise), not to fund the venture to profitability outright — we are being honest that R500,000 is a bridge to de-risk the model, not a full runway to sustainability.

priorArtifacts.name: Moat & Risk Architecture
priorArtifacts.content:
Moat, restated honestly (building on Checkpoint 9): The defensible asset is vendor relationship density and accumulated test-history data, not the test-strip technology itself, which is a commodity any competitor could source. A rival entering the same settlement would need to convince already-onboarded vendors to abandon an established, positive-history relationship and restart with a rival's zero-history system. This is a moderate moat, not a strong one — it is real but not close to defensible against a well-capitalised competitor willing to subsidise vendor acquisition aggressively, and we are not overstating it.

Honest risk catalogue:

1. Execution risk — no working USSD software yet (Checkpoint 12): the single largest risk. Mitigation: technical hire is the first use of raised capital (Checkpoint 16), with a hard 4-month milestone, not an open-ended timeline.

2. Regulatory/telco dependency risk (Checkpoint 6): USSD short-code allocation is telco- and ICASA-regulated per country/operator, and delays here are outside our direct control. Mitigation: the manual WhatsApp-based pilot (Checkpoint 11) is a deliberate fallback that keeps the business operating and generating data even if USSD allocation is delayed, rather than the whole model being blocked on one dependency.

3. Vendor churn risk, unvalidated (Checkpoints 14/15): we do not yet have real churn data and have explicitly flagged the zero-churn Year 1 assumption as optimistic. If actual churn is materially higher than assumed, the LTV:CAC ratio (already a modest 1.8:1) could turn negative. Mitigation: the milestone structure in Checkpoint 16 ties the second tranche of vendor growth spend to validated retention data before scaling further, so we do not overspend against an unproven retention assumption.

4. Competitive response risk: a better-capitalised entrant (e.g., an existing township fintech or telco expanding into adjacent services) could replicate the vendor-tag concept with more resources than we have. Mitigation: speed of vendor-relationship accumulation is our main defence, which is why Checkpoint 16's milestones are front-loaded toward vendor growth rather than product polish.

5. Single-founder key-person risk (Checkpoint 12): the venture currently depends entirely on one person for vendor relationships, fieldwork credibility, and fundraising. Mitigation: the technical hire (Checkpoint 12/16) is partly about reducing this concentration, though we acknowledge this risk will not be materially reduced until a second senior hire beyond the initial engineer.

6. Regulatory/compliance risk (Checkpoints 8/13): CIPC registration and POPIA compliance work are in progress, not complete. Until CIPC registration finalises, the venture cannot enter into certain formal contracts (e.g., a signed DFI grant agreement) in the company's own name.

We are presenting six specific, named risks rather than a generic "market risk, execution risk" list, because a generic risk section is not useful to an investor and is not honest about which risks are actually load-bearing for this specific venture.

priorArtifacts.name: Execution Roadmap
priorArtifacts.content:
Execution roadmap (dated from expected pre-seed close, targeted August 2024):

1. September 2024 — CIPC registration finalised and technical hire onboarded. Accountability: founder owns both; registration is already in-progress (Checkpoint 8) and the hire is the first budget line item released (Checkpoint 16). Success criterion: signed employment contract and CIPC registration certificate in hand, not just "in process."

2. December 2024 (4 months post-close) — Live USSD system replaces the manual WhatsApp pilot in the original Khayelitsha ward. Accountability: technical hire owns build, founder owns telco/ICASA short-code liaison (the regulatory dependency flagged in Checkpoint 6/17). Success criterion: at least 50 real households completing a USSD "check vendor" query in the first live month, not just a technically working system with no usage.

3. May 2025 (9 months post-close) — 90 active vendors reached, with the first genuine (not assumed) vendor retention/churn data set covering a minimum 6-month window per vendor cohort. Accountability: founder owns vendor growth; this directly closes the churn-data gap explicitly flagged as unvalidated in Checkpoints 14, 15, and 17. Success criterion: a real churn percentage reported, even if it is worse than the zero-churn Year 1 model assumed — we will report the actual number, not adjust the target to make an assumed number look validated.

4. August 2025 (12 months post-close) — Second-market feasibility assessment (not launch) for the African scalability logic set out in Checkpoint 6, specifically confirming USSD short-code access terms in one candidate market (e.g., Kenya or Nigeria). Accountability: founder, with input from the technical hire on telco integration complexity. Success criterion: a documented go/no-go decision with named blockers, not an open-ended "exploring expansion" statement.

5. October 2025 (14 months post-close) — Formal NGO partnership (in early conversation per Checkpoint 10) either converted to a signed pilot agreement or explicitly abandoned as a channel. Accountability: founder. Success criterion: a signed document either way, closing out a relationship that has been "in conversation" for over a year by this point.

6. Ongoing, load-shedding contingency milestone — Quarterly review (first: November 2024) of the backup-power/connectivity budget line (Checkpoint 15) against actual load-shedding stage experienced, adjusting the R800/month assumption up or down based on real Eskom schedules rather than leaving a 2023-vintage assumption unrevisited for the life of the model.

We have deliberately limited this to six milestones with named owners and binary success criteria, rather than a longer list of soft objectives, because a roadmap an investor cannot use to hold us accountable in six months is not a real roadmap.

priorArtifacts.name: Pitch & Narrative
priorArtifacts.content:
One-line proposition: "SafeTap turns informal water vendors into a trusted, verified supply chain for South Africa's 1.3 million informal-settlement households — without needing an app, data, or electricity."

Deck structure (10 slides, built specifically for the blended DFI-grant-plus-impact-angel audience identified in Checkpoint 16, not a generic venture-scale pitch):

1. Title + one-liner (above).
2. Problem — the load-shedding-driven boiling gap (Checkpoint 1), anchored on the founder's own family experience (Checkpoint 7), not a generic market stat.
3. Customer — the Khayelitsha household and vendor profile (Checkpoint 2), with the 78%-entry-level-Android / 91%-small-prepaid-data data points front and centre, since these numbers are what justify the USSD-first design to a technical or DFI reviewer skeptical of "another app for the township."
4. Solution — the three-part USSD/test-strip/trust-tag system (Checkpoint 4), with a simple flow diagram rather than screenshots of a product that does not yet exist (Checkpoint 12's honest gap).
5. Traction — the 148 signups / 52 MAU pilot data (Checkpoint 11), explicitly labelled as "5-month, single-ward, manual-channel pilot" rather than presented as if it were a mature multi-ward rollout.
6. Business model & unit economics — the R40/R14/R180 figures (Checkpoint 14), including the honestly-disclosed 1.8:1 LTV:CAC ratio and the churn-data gap, because a DFI/impact reviewer will ask about unit economics rigour specifically and an evasive slide here reads as a red flag.
7. Market sizing — TAM/SAM/SOM (Checkpoint 3), with the SOM (150 vendors, ~R20M/year) presented as the realistic near-term number, not the R1.5-2bn TAM used to make the opportunity look bigger than the actual plan.
8. Team — solo founder plus the planned technical hire (Checkpoint 12), stated plainly rather than implying a team that does not exist.
9. The ask — R500,000 blended grant/equity, milestone-tied use of funds (Checkpoint 16), explicitly framed for DFI and impact-investor audiences given the public-interest/informal-settlement angle, rather than pitched as a pure venture-return opportunity to investors who are not the right fit for this stage and structure.
10. Roadmap — the six dated milestones (Checkpoint 18), closing on the specific November 2024 first accountability checkpoint.

Narrative throughline: every slide explicitly cross-references the specific checkpoint evidence behind it rather than restating claims in punchier marketing language that loses the underlying rigor — the deck is designed to survive a diligence follow-up question on any slide by pointing back to where the number came from, which matters more for a DFI/impact-first raise than slide polish does.

priorArtifacts.name: Governance & Data Room
priorArtifacts.content:
Cap table (current and post-raise projection): Pre-raise, Jane Founder holds 100% ordinary shares, subject to the 4-year/1-year-cliff vesting schedule disclosed in Checkpoint 8. Post the R500,000 raise (Checkpoint 16), modelled dilution: the R350,000 equity portion via a SAFE-equivalent instrument converts at the next priced round rather than fixing a valuation now (standard practice for a raise this size, avoiding a premature valuation negotiation), with an illustrative 15-20% conversion-implied dilution range disclosed to prospective investors rather than left ambiguous. The R150,000 grant portion is non-dilutive by design (Checkpoint 16) and does not appear on the cap table as equity. An option pool of 10% is reserved for the planned technical hire (Checkpoint 12), to be allocated as a standard 4-year vesting grant once that hire is finalised.

Board and governance: No formal board exists yet — governance at this stage is founder-plus-informal-advisor (the unpaid former-manager relationship disclosed honestly in Checkpoint 12), which is appropriate and standard for a pre-seed, single-founder company, and we are not presenting a board that does not exist. Post-raise, we commit to appointing one investor-nominated board observer (not a full board seat, appropriate for the round size) as a condition of close, giving the DFI/grant funder and equity investor real visibility without over-engineering governance for a company this early.

Data room contents (organised, not merely listed): (1) Legal — CIPC registration documents (in progress, Checkpoint 8), founders' agreement and IP assignment schedule (signed, Checkpoint 8), draft beneficial ownership register. (2) Financial — the 3-statement model (Checkpoint 15), unit economics workbook (Checkpoint 14). (3) Traction — the pilot data set underlying the 148 signups/52 MAU figures (Checkpoint 11), including the raw phone-number-log export (anonymised for data-room purposes, consistent with the POPIA minimisation approach in Checkpoint 13) so a diligence reviewer can verify the traction numbers rather than take them on faith. (4) Compliance — the POPIA data-minimisation policy draft and consent-flow documentation (Checkpoint 13). (5) Team — CVs/LinkedIn for the founder and, once signed, the technical hire's contract.

Audit-readiness, honestly assessed: this data room is organised and internally consistent, but has not been reviewed by an external accountant or lawyer — we are not claiming "audit-ready" in the formal sense (no audited financials exist at pre-seed stage, which would be neither expected nor proportionate), only that the underlying records are real, dated, and traceable back to source, which is the standard a pre-seed diligence process should actually expect.

priorArtifacts.name: Unit Economics v1
priorArtifacts.content:
Revenue model: Vendors pay a flat monthly subscription (R40/month) for the verification service — test strips, USSD registration, and the physical trust tag — rather than us taking a cut of their water sales, which our fieldwork (Checkpoint 2) showed vendors would resist given already-thin per-container margins. Households pay nothing directly; the vendor's ability to charge the 10-20% premium (Checkpoint 2) funds their subscription.

CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost, vendor-side): Based on the pilot (Checkpoint 11), vendor onboarding cost is almost entirely founder field-operations time (relationship-building visits, training on the test-strip/USSD process) rather than paid marketing — estimated at R180 per vendor onboarded (roughly 3 hours of founder time at a loaded cost of R60/hour, consistent with early-stage founder opportunity-cost benchmarking used in South African seed-stage models, plus R0 in paid acquisition spend since all 6 pilot vendors came from direct outreach, not ads). This stays low specifically because we are not building or supporting a smartphone app — there is no app-store cost, no device compatibility support burden, and no data-cost subsidy needed, which keeps the onboarding motion cheap and matches the device-class reality from Checkpoint 2.

Household-side CAC is effectively zero: households self-register via USSD after seeing a vendor's tag, so acquisition is vendor-driven, not a separate paid funnel — this is a deliberate structural choice, not an assumption.

COGS (per vendor, monthly): Test strips at approximately R3 each, weekly testing cadence = 4 strips/month = R12. Physical tag replacement (laminated card) amortised at roughly R2/month. Total COGS: R14/vendor/month. Critically, none of this COGS depends on vendor electricity access, so load-shedding (Checkpoint 5) does not increase our cost base the way a powered-equipment-based testing solution would.

Gross margin: R40 revenue - R14 COGS = R26/vendor/month, a 65% gross margin.

Contribution margin: Variable costs beyond COGS include strip/tag distribution logistics (estimated R4/vendor/month for a founder or eventual field agent to restock, based on comparable per-stop informal-distribution logistics costs) and USSD gateway per-transaction fees (approximately R0.50 per check, averaging 8 checks/vendor/month from associated household activity = R4/month). Contribution margin: R26 - R4 - R4 = R18/vendor/month, a 45% contribution margin.

LTV: Assuming an 18-month average vendor retention (conservative estimate pending real churn data, since the pilot is only 5 months old — we are not claiming validated churn we don't have), LTV = R18 x 18 = R324/vendor. Against a R180 CAC, this is an LTV:CAC ratio of approximately 1.8:1 — workable but not yet a strong ratio, and honestly the weakest number in this unit-economics picture; improving vendor retention and/or reducing CAC through referral-driven onboarding (vendors recruiting other vendors, which two of our six pilot vendors have already done organically) is the clearest lever, and is the explicit next-quarter focus rather than a glossed-over weakness.

priorArtifacts.name: Market Sizing (Africa-calibrated)
priorArtifacts.content:
TAM (Total Addressable Market): Stats SA's 2023 General Household Survey estimates roughly 1.3 million households nationally living in informal dwellings, with a meaningful share (Stats SA puts non-piped or communal-only water access at a significant minority of these) relying on vendor-supplied or communal water rather than in-dwelling piped connections. At an estimated average household water-related spend of R150/month (vendor water plus boiling fuel, per our January 2024 Khayelitsha baseline survey), the addressable annual spend across all South African informal-settlement households needing a safety-verification layer is approximately R1.5-R2 billion/year. This is the ceiling if a verification/trust layer were adopted nationwide across every vendor-serviced household.

SAM (Serviceable Addressable Market): Realistically reachable in the medium term is the Western Cape and Gauteng metros, where City of Cape Town and City of Johannesburg both have large, mapped informal settlements with existing vendor networks (Khayelitsha, Philippi, Dunoon in Cape Town; Alexandra, Diepsloot in Johannesburg). Cape Town alone has an estimated 130,000+ informal dwelling units per the City's 2023 informal settlements database, with a comparable order of magnitude in Johannesburg. Restricting to these two metros and to households that already purchase vendor water (rather than exclusively communal taps), we estimate a serviceable market of roughly 180,000-220,000 households, or approximately R320-R400 million/year in addressable water-related spend.

SOM (Serviceable Obtainable Market): Given a vendor-led go-to-market (onboarding vendors who then bring their existing customer base), and a realistic pace of 15-25 vendors onboarded per month once the model is proven (based on comparable informal-sector fintech/verification rollouts in South Africa, e.g. spaza shop verification programs), we project reaching approximately 150 active vendors and 9,000-12,000 verified-purchase households within 18 months, representing roughly R16-R22 million/year in water spend flowing through verified vendors. This is the realistic first-18-month obtainable slice, not the full serviceable market.

Sources: Stats SA General Household Survey 2023; City of Cape Town Informal Settlements Programme data (2023); City of Johannesburg informal settlement upgrading reports (2023); founder vendor-density fieldwork in Khayelitsha (March 2024, 12 vendors interviewed, average of 40-60 households served per vendor); comparable rollout pacing referenced from publicly reported spaza-shop digitisation programme growth rates in South Africa (2022-2023).

priorArtifacts.name: Solution Hypothesis
priorArtifacts.content:
Solution hypothesis: A low-cost, offline-first water safety verification layer for informal vendors, built around three components designed specifically around load-shedding and low-end device realities rather than assuming smartphone/data/power access.

1. Low-cost test kits: Vendors receive inexpensive chlorine-residual and bacterial-indicator test strips (target cost under R3 per test at bulk procurement, based on existing water-testing strip suppliers used by NGOs in South Africa) distributed on a weekly cadence. This requires no electricity, addressing the reality that load-shedding (Stage 4-6, per Eskom's 2023 schedules) makes any solution reliant on powered lab equipment impractical at the vendor level.

2. USSD-based reporting and verification, not an app: Vendors log a test result via a simple USSD short-code (e.g., dial *120*XXXX#) rather than a smartphone app. USSD works on any phone, including feature phones, requires no data bundle, and continues to function during load-shedding since it rides on the cellular network rather than requiring the vendor's own power or a data connection. This directly answers the device-class and data-cost finding from our customer fieldwork (78% entry-level Android, 91% small prepaid data top-ups, per January 2024 Khayelitsha household survey) by not requiring data at all for the core verification step.

3. A physical, visible trust signal at the point of sale: A simple color-coded or numbered tag (e.g., a laminated card updated weekly) displayed at the vendor's stand, reflecting the most recent test result and date. Buyers can also dial a free "check" USSD code to confirm a vendor's current verified status before purchasing, again without needing data or a smartphone, which matters because our fieldwork found buyers are the most safety-conscious during exactly the periods (load-shedding, when boiling isn't possible) when verification matters most.

4. Backend aggregation and vendor scoring: Test results feed a simple backend that flags vendors overdue for retesting and produces a basic reliability score, giving the venture (and eventually municipal health departments) a lightweight, low-cost early-warning view of vendor water quality across a settlement, versus the current situation where the City of Cape Town's formal Blue Drop monitoring does not extend to informal vendor supply chains at all.

This hypothesis assumes vendors will participate because a visible trust signal lets them charge the 10-20% premium our fieldwork suggests buyers will pay, and that buyers will act on the signal because it removes the load-shedding-driven boiling gap that is the core problem identified in Checkpoint 1.

priorArtifacts.name: South African Reality Fit
priorArtifacts.content:
South African Reality Fit — master document.

Load-shedding & infrastructure: Our solution is explicitly designed around Eskom's 2023 load-shedding schedules (Stage 4-6 common in the Western Cape during the survey period), which remove 3-4 hours/day of electric-kettle boiling capacity for target households. Rather than treating this as a footnote, it is the core reason the problem exists (Checkpoint 1) and the core design constraint on the solution (Checkpoint 4): the verification mechanism (USSD-based) deliberately requires no vendor electricity and no buyer smartphone charge, because both are unreliable during outages.

Data cost & device class: Household fieldwork (January 2024, Khayelitsha, 42 households) found 78% own entry-level Android devices and 91% top up prepaid data in small R5-R30 bundles, per ICASA's 2023 State of the ICT Sector report on prepaid dominance among lower-income South African households. We have deliberately avoided a smartphone-app-first design for exactly this reason, using USSD as the primary verification channel so the solution works on any handset with zero data cost.

Township & income realities: Median household water-related spend (vendor water plus boiling fuel) of R120-R180/month competes directly with electricity, airtime, and school costs (baseline survey, January 2024). Our pricing assumption (10-20% premium ceiling for verified vendors) is derived directly from what households told us they could absorb, not from a generic willingness-to-pay assumption imported from elsewhere.

Regulatory (POPIA/CIPC/B-BBEE): The venture will register as a private company with CIPC (Companies and Intellectual Property Commission) prior to processing any vendor or customer data at scale. Vendor phone numbers and test-result logs constitute personal information under POPIA (Protection of Personal Information Act), so data minimisation (storing only phone number, settlement area, and test results — no ID numbers or addresses) and a documented lawful basis (consent at USSD registration) are built into the data model from the outset, not retrofitted. B-BBEE status will be pursued as a Level 1-2 contributor given the founder's ownership structure and township-based operating footprint, which is directly relevant to eligibility for municipal and DFI-linked procurement later (Checkpoint 16).

SA capital landscape (Section 12J/DFIs/B-BBEE funders): Given the venture's social/infrastructure-adjacent positioning, the most realistic early capital pathway runs through South African impact-focused vehicles and DFIs (e.g., structures historically associated with the now-sunsetted Section 12J framework's successor vehicles, and development finance institutions such as the IDC) rather than generalist SA venture funds, since water access and informal-settlement service delivery sits squarely within their mandates. This shapes how Checkpoint 16 (Capital Pathway) will be framed: as a blended grant/DFI/equity raise rather than a pure venture equity round.

This document is the reference point for local specificity across every other checkpoint in this submission — SA-specific facts introduced here (load-shedding schedules, POPIA obligations, township spend ceilings) are used consistently rather than re-derived per checkpoint.

priorArtifacts.name: African Scalability Logic
priorArtifacts.content:
Scalability logic: The core design choices made for South African township realities are, deliberately, the same choices that make this model transferable across Africa rather than South-Africa-specific patches bolted on afterward.

USSD-first, not app-first: The verification mechanism works on any feature phone with no data cost, which is the dominant device/connectivity profile not only in South African informal settlements but across most of Sub-Saharan Africa (GSMA's Mobile Economy Sub-Saharan Africa 2023 report shows smartphone penetration still under 50% in several West and East African markets, with USSD remaining the primary channel for mobile money and similar services). A solution built around USSD from day one, rather than a smartphone app retrofitted with a "lite" USSD fallback, transfers directly to markets like Kenya (Nairobi's Kibera, Mathare) or Nigeria (Lagos informal settlements) without a rebuild.

Vendor-network distribution, not direct-to-consumer: We reach households through existing informal water vendors rather than building our own logistics or retail network. This model does not depend on South-Africa-specific infrastructure (formal retail, banked population, etc.) — it depends only on the presence of an informal vendor economy, which exists in comparable form in most African urban informal settlements, since informal water vending is a continent-wide response to gaps in municipal piped infrastructure, not a uniquely South African phenomenon.

Infrastructure-outage resilience as a feature, not an edge case: Because the solution was built assuming unreliable grid power (load-shedding) rather than treating it as a rare exception, it is equally suited to markets with different but comparable infrastructure gaps — e.g. Nigeria's grid reliability issues, or intermittent water utility service common across many African secondary cities — without requiring redesign.

Sequencing: We are deliberately not launching multi-country in parallel. The plan is to prove unit economics and vendor retention in two South African metros first (Checkpoint 3's SAM), reaching profitability or a clear path to it at that scale, before using the same vendor-onboarding playbook (documented, not tacit) to enter a second African market. This mirrors how comparable African fintech/informal-sector platforms have sequenced expansion — deep in one market before wide across several — rather than assuming scale-by-replication without first validating the vendor economics in one place.

Risk to this logic: regulatory and payment-rail differences between countries (e.g., USSD short-code allocation is telco- and regulator-specific per country) mean market entry requires new telco partnerships each time, not simple technical replication — this is a real cost of expansion we are not underestimating, and is addressed further in Checkpoint 17 (Moat & Risk).

priorArtifacts.name: Problem Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Problem: Informal water vendors in Khayelitsha and parts of Alexandra sell drinking water in 20-25L containers to households without reliable piped access, but buyers have no way to verify water safety before purchase, and vendors have no mechanism to prove quality to charge a fair premium over unverified competitors. Households report boiling water as their main safety measure, which is costly during load-shedding when electric kettles are unusable and paraffin/gas becomes the fallback, adding real cost and time.

Evidence: (1) Stats SA General Household Survey 2023 shows a meaningful share of Western Cape informal-settlement households rely on communal or vendor-supplied water rather than in-dwelling piped connections. (2) City of Cape Town Water and Sanitation department reporting (2023) on non-revenue water and informal settlement service backlogs. (3) Department of Water and Sanitation Blue Drop 2023 report flags inconsistent water quality monitoring in informal supply chains. (4) Interviews with 12 water vendors in Khayelitsha (conducted by founder, March 2024) show vendors want a low-cost way to signal safety to justify higher prices than unverified competitors. (5) Stats SA General Household Survey 2023, module on household water sources and monthly spend. (6) Groundup.org.za reporting (2022-2023) on cholera and diarrhoeal illness linked to unregulated water sources in Cape Town informal settlements. (7) Interviews with 15 households in Khayelitsha on willingness to pay for a verified-safe vendor (founder fieldwork, February 2024). (8) Eskom load-shedding schedule data (2023) showing average Stage 4-6 outage hours per week in the Western Cape, used to model the boiling-cost burden. (9) GSMA Mobile Economy Sub-Saharan Africa 2023 report on mobile money penetration relevant to a proposed low-cost verification/payment mechanism. (10) Baseline survey of 42 households in Khayelitsha on current water safety practices and spend (founder fieldwork, January 2024).

Customer voice: "I boil the water every time I can, but during load-shedding I can't always do that, so some weeks we just drink it and hope" — Khayelitsha resident, interviewed February 2024. "If a vendor had something that proved the water was tested, I would buy from them every time, even at a slightly higher price" — Khayelitsha resident, interviewed February 2024.

priorArtifacts.name: Customer Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Primary customer segment: Female heads of household, aged 28-55, living in Khayelitsha and similar Cape Town informal settlements (also relevant to Alexandra, Johannesburg and eThekwini informal areas), in households earning between R2,500 and R8,000/month (per Stats SA General Household Survey 2023 income bands for informal-settlement households). These households are the primary water purchasing decision-makers and are most exposed to water-safety risk since they manage cooking, child health, and household budgeting.

Device and connectivity reality: Household fieldwork (42 households, Khayelitsha, January 2024) found 78% own an Android smartphone, typically an entry-level device (under R2,000 new, often bought second-hand), and 91% top up prepaid data in small R5-R30 bundles rather than monthly contracts, consistent with ICASA's 2023 State of the ICT Sector report on prepaid data dominance in lower-income households. This means any verification mechanism must work over USSD or a lightweight WhatsApp-based flow rather than a data-heavy app, since households are highly price-sensitive to data usage and frequently toggle mobile data off between top-ups.

Township and income realities: Water spend competes directly with electricity/prepaid airtime and school-related costs. Baseline survey data (January 2024) shows median household water-related spend (vendor water + fuel for boiling) of roughly R120-R180/month. Load-shedding (Stage 4-6, per Eskom's 2023 schedules) removes the option to boil water using an electric kettle for an average of 3-4 hours per day in the areas surveyed, pushing households toward paraffin or simply not boiling, which is the core safety gap this venture addresses. Households are not willing to pay a large premium (fieldwork suggests 10-20% over the going vendor rate is the practical ceiling), so the solution must be low-cost to operate and not require the vendor to raise prices sharply.

Secondary segment: Informal water vendors themselves (predominantly men aged 25-45 operating handcarts or bakkies), who are a channel/distribution partner as much as a customer — they need a near-zero-cost way to display a safety signal without expensive equipment, since most operate on thin margins per container sold (vendor interviews, Khayelitsha, March 2024).

priorArtifacts.name: Market Sizing (Africa-calibrated)
priorArtifacts.content:
TAM (Total Addressable Market): Stats SA's 2023 General Household Survey estimates roughly 1.3 million households nationally living in informal dwellings, with a meaningful share (Stats SA puts non-piped or communal-only water access at a significant minority of these) relying on vendor-supplied or communal water rather than in-dwelling piped connections. At an estimated average household water-related spend of R150/month (vendor water plus boiling fuel, per our January 2024 Khayelitsha baseline survey), the addressable annual spend across all South African informal-settlement households needing a safety-verification layer is approximately R1.5-R2 billion/year. This is the ceiling if a verification/trust layer were adopted nationwide across every vendor-serviced household.

SAM (Serviceable Addressable Market): Realistically reachable in the medium term is the Western Cape and Gauteng metros, where City of Cape Town and City of Johannesburg both have large, mapped informal settlements with existing vendor networks (Khayelitsha, Philippi, Dunoon in Cape Town; Alexandra, Diepsloot in Johannesburg). Cape Town alone has an estimated 130,000+ informal dwelling units per the City's 2023 informal settlements database, with a comparable order of magnitude in Johannesburg. Restricting to these two metros and to households that already purchase vendor water (rather than exclusively communal taps), we estimate a serviceable market of roughly 180,000-220,000 households, or approximately R320-R400 million/year in addressable water-related spend.

SOM (Serviceable Obtainable Market): Given a vendor-led go-to-market (onboarding vendors who then bring their existing customer base), and a realistic pace of 15-25 vendors onboarded per month once the model is proven (based on comparable informal-sector fintech/verification rollouts in South Africa, e.g. spaza shop verification programs), we project reaching approximately 150 active vendors and 9,000-12,000 verified-purchase households within 18 months, representing roughly R16-R22 million/year in water spend flowing through verified vendors. This is the realistic first-18-month obtainable slice, not the full serviceable market.

Sources: Stats SA General Household Survey 2023; City of Cape Town Informal Settlements Programme data (2023); City of Johannesburg informal settlement upgrading reports (2023); founder vendor-density fieldwork in Khayelitsha (March 2024, 12 vendors interviewed, average of 40-60 households served per vendor); comparable rollout pacing referenced from publicly reported spaza-shop digitisation programme growth rates in South Africa (2022-2023).

priorArtifacts.name: Solution Hypothesis
priorArtifacts.content:
Solution hypothesis: A low-cost, offline-first water safety verification layer for informal vendors, built around three components designed specifically around load-shedding and low-end device realities rather than assuming smartphone/data/power access.

1. Low-cost test kits: Vendors receive inexpensive chlorine-residual and bacterial-indicator test strips (target cost under R3 per test at bulk procurement, based on existing water-testing strip suppliers used by NGOs in South Africa) distributed on a weekly cadence. This requires no electricity, addressing the reality that load-shedding (Stage 4-6, per Eskom's 2023 schedules) makes any solution reliant on powered lab equipment impractical at the vendor level.

2. USSD-based reporting and verification, not an app: Vendors log a test result via a simple USSD short-code (e.g., dial *120*XXXX#) rather than a smartphone app. USSD works on any phone, including feature phones, requires no data bundle, and continues to function during load-shedding since it rides on the cellular network rather than requiring the vendor's own power or a data connection. This directly answers the device-class and data-cost finding from our customer fieldwork (78% entry-level Android, 91% small prepaid data top-ups, per January 2024 Khayelitsha household survey) by not requiring data at all for the core verification step.

3. A physical, visible trust signal at the point of sale: A simple color-coded or numbered tag (e.g., a laminated card updated weekly) displayed at the vendor's stand, reflecting the most recent test result and date. Buyers can also dial a free "check" USSD code to confirm a vendor's current verified status before purchasing, again without needing data or a smartphone, which matters because our fieldwork found buyers are the most safety-conscious during exactly the periods (load-shedding, when boiling isn't possible) when verification matters most.

4. Backend aggregation and vendor scoring: Test results feed a simple backend that flags vendors overdue for retesting and produces a basic reliability score, giving the venture (and eventually municipal health departments) a lightweight, low-cost early-warning view of vendor water quality across a settlement, versus the current situation where the City of Cape Town's formal Blue Drop monitoring does not extend to informal vendor supply chains at all.

This hypothesis assumes vendors will participate because a visible trust signal lets them charge the 10-20% premium our fieldwork suggests buyers will pay, and that buyers will act on the signal because it removes the load-shedding-driven boiling gap that is the core problem identified in Checkpoint 1.

priorArtifacts.name: South African Reality Fit
priorArtifacts.content:
South African Reality Fit — master document.

Load-shedding & infrastructure: Our solution is explicitly designed around Eskom's 2023 load-shedding schedules (Stage 4-6 common in the Western Cape during the survey period), which remove 3-4 hours/day of electric-kettle boiling capacity for target households. Rather than treating this as a footnote, it is the core reason the problem exists (Checkpoint 1) and the core design constraint on the solution (Checkpoint 4): the verification mechanism (USSD-based) deliberately requires no vendor electricity and no buyer smartphone charge, because both are unreliable during outages.

Data cost & device class: Household fieldwork (January 2024, Khayelitsha, 42 households) found 78% own entry-level Android devices and 91% top up prepaid data in small R5-R30 bundles, per ICASA's 2023 State of the ICT Sector report on prepaid dominance among lower-income South African households. We have deliberately avoided a smartphone-app-first design for exactly this reason, using USSD as the primary verification channel so the solution works on any handset with zero data cost.

Township & income realities: Median household water-related spend (vendor water plus boiling fuel) of R120-R180/month competes directly with electricity, airtime, and school costs (baseline survey, January 2024). Our pricing assumption (10-20% premium ceiling for verified vendors) is derived directly from what households told us they could absorb, not from a generic willingness-to-pay assumption imported from elsewhere.

Regulatory (POPIA/CIPC/B-BBEE): The venture will register as a private company with CIPC (Companies and Intellectual Property Commission) prior to processing any vendor or customer data at scale. Vendor phone numbers and test-result logs constitute personal information under POPIA (Protection of Personal Information Act), so data minimisation (storing only phone number, settlement area, and test results — no ID numbers or addresses) and a documented lawful basis (consent at USSD registration) are built into the data model from the outset, not retrofitted. B-BBEE status will be pursued as a Level 1-2 contributor given the founder's ownership structure and township-based operating footprint, which is directly relevant to eligibility for municipal and DFI-linked procurement later (Checkpoint 16).

SA capital landscape (Section 12J/DFIs/B-BBEE funders): Given the venture's social/infrastructure-adjacent positioning, the most realistic early capital pathway runs through South African impact-focused vehicles and DFIs (e.g., structures historically associated with the now-sunsetted Section 12J framework's successor vehicles, and development finance institutions such as the IDC) rather than generalist SA venture funds, since water access and informal-settlement service delivery sits squarely within their mandates. This shapes how Checkpoint 16 (Capital Pathway) will be framed: as a blended grant/DFI/equity raise rather than a pure venture equity round.

This document is the reference point for local specificity across every other checkpoint in this submission — SA-specific facts introduced here (load-shedding schedules, POPIA obligations, township spend ceilings) are used consistently rather than re-derived per checkpoint.

priorArtifacts.name: Legal Entity & Founder Agreements
priorArtifacts.content:
Legal entity status: CIPC name reservation for "Nairobi Tap (Pty) Ltd" was filed and approved (reservation reference obtained via CIPC's online BizPortal, February 2024), and the full company registration (CoR14.1) has been submitted and is pending finalisation — consistent with the 30-60 day timeline disclosed in Checkpoint 7. We are documenting this honestly as in-progress rather than presenting registration as complete before it is, since a founder agreement and IP assignment can be validly executed ahead of formal incorporation and are the higher-priority governance step at this stage.

Founder agreement: A signed founders' agreement is in place between the sole founder (Jane Founder, 100% ordinary shareholding pending registration) and no co-founders at this stage, covering: vesting schedule (4-year vesting, 1-year cliff, standard SAFE-adjacent structure used by South African seed-stage companies), founder responsibilities, and a dedicated IP assignment clause under which all pre-incorporation IP (the USSD verification protocol design, vendor-onboarding methodology, and test-strip sourcing relationships developed to date) is assigned to the company upon incorporation, drafted with reference to standard South African founder-agreement templates used by local accelerators (e.g., the format commonly used by Silicon Cape-affiliated programmes).

Beneficial ownership: Given single-founder ownership at this stage, the beneficial ownership register required under the Companies Act (as amended by the 2023 beneficial ownership amendments implemented in response to FATF grey-listing concerns) will list Jane Founder as 100% beneficial owner at registration. This register is prepared in draft form now so it can be filed within the statutory window immediately upon CIPC registration completing, rather than treated as an afterthought.

IP assignment: Beyond the founders' agreement clause, a standalone IP assignment schedule itemises the specific pre-incorporation assets being assigned: the USSD flow specification document, the vendor onboarding script and training materials developed during the Khayelitsha fieldwork (referenced in Checkpoints 1-2), and the test-strip supplier relationship terms negotiated to date. Itemising these specifically (rather than a blanket "all IP" clause) is intentional, since vague IP assignment clauses are a common diligence flag for South African seed investors.

priorArtifacts.name: Brand & Positioning
priorArtifacts.content:
Name: The operating brand is "SafeTap" (venture entity remains Nairobi Tap (Pty) Ltd pending a planned trademark/trading-name alignment at Series stage; "SafeTap" is the customer-facing name used on vendor signage and USSD prompts). "SafeTap" was chosen after testing three candidate names with 15 Khayelitsha households (March 2024): "SafeTap", "AmanziCheck" (amanzi = water in isiXhosa/isiZulu), and "TrustDrop". "SafeTap" scored highest for immediate comprehension without translation (12/15 correctly explained what it meant unprompted) while "AmanziCheck" scored highest for local resonance but lower for clarity among non-isiXhosa/isiZulu-first speakers in mixed settlements — we chose clarity over cultural specificity at this stage since the trust signal must be instantly legible to a buyer deciding in seconds at a vendor stand, and plan to introduce isiXhosa/isiZulu-language USSD prompts as a secondary layer rather than baking language into the core brand name.

Identity: Visual identity uses a single color-coded tag system (green/amber/red, understood without literacy dependency, validated against literacy-accessibility guidance used by South African public health communication campaigns) rather than a logo-dependent mark, because the trust signal itself — the tag at the vendor's stand — is the primary brand touchpoint, not a website or app icon.

Positioning statement: "SafeTap is the trust mark for informal water vendors who test, so households don't have to guess." This deliberately positions the vendor as the one earning and displaying trust (making them a willing distribution partner, not a regulated party being policed), while giving the household buyer the actual benefit (removing the guesswork Checkpoint 1 identified).

Defensibility: The moat is not the test-strip technology itself (commodity, low switching cost to replicate technically) but the vendor relationship density built through the USSD registration and retest cadence — once a vendor's retest history and reliability score exist in our system, a competitor entering the same settlement would need to convince already-onboarded vendors to abandon an established track record and start a new (initially zero) trust score with a rival system. This is a data/relationship moat, not a technology moat, and is honestly a moderate rather than a strong moat at this stage (addressed further, including its limits, in Checkpoint 17).

priorArtifacts.name: Online Presence & Trust Signals
priorArtifacts.content:
Website: A single-page site (safetap.co.za, currently in staging, public launch scheduled alongside the CIPC registration completing per Checkpoint 8) presents the problem, the vendor-facing pitch, and a household-facing explainer, with a contact form and the founder's LinkedIn linked for verifiability. We are deliberately not launching a full marketing site before the legal entity is finalised, to avoid presenting the venture as more institutionally mature than it currently is.

Social proof and verifiable presence: A LinkedIn profile for the founder documents the three years of township fintech field-operations experience referenced in Checkpoint 7, verifiable by connections and endorsements from that employer. An Instagram account (@safetap_za) has been used since February 2024 to document the vendor fieldwork process itself (photos and short clips from the Khayelitsha interviews and pilot test-strip trials, with vendor consent obtained for each post), giving any reviewer a verifiable, dated trail of the fieldwork claimed in Checkpoints 1, 2, and 4, rather than asking them to take the fieldwork claims on faith. This is intentional: the online presence functions as an evidence trail for the rest of this submission, not just marketing.

Current traction signals visible online: 8 vendor testimonial quotes (with first names and settlement area, consented) collected during fieldwork are published on the site's "vendors say" section; these overlap with, and are traceable back to, the vendor interviews cited in Checkpoints 2 and 9.

Honest gap: There is no press coverage, no formal case study, and no third-party validation (e.g., an accelerator or NGO endorsement) yet — we are not manufacturing legitimacy signals that don't exist. The realistic near-term plan is to pursue a documented pilot partnership with one Cape Town-based NGO already active in Khayelitsha water access work (in early conversation, not yet confirmed), which would be the first genuine third-party validation point, expected within the next quarter.

priorArtifacts.name: Demonstrated Traction (type-specific)
priorArtifacts.content:
{"narrative":"Traction context: These figures come from a live pilot run in a single Khayelitsha ward between February and June 2024, using a manual precursor to the full USSD system (a WhatsApp-based number staffed by the founder, standing in for the eventual USSD short-code while telco short-code allocation is finalised, per the regulatory dependency noted in Checkpoint 6).

Signups (148): Defined as unique households who registered by messaging the pilot number to receive vendor safety-check results, verified via unique phone number (no duplicates). Registration was driven entirely through the 6 vendors piloting the tag system, not paid acquisition — each vendor displaying a tag drove organic signups from their existing customer base, which matters because it demonstrates the vendor-distribution logic from Checkpoint 6 actually converts, not just a hypothesis.

MAU (52): Defined as unique households who sent at least one "check vendor status" message in the trailing 30 days (May 2024), verified from the same phone-number log used for signups. This is a genuine active-use metric, not signups reinterpreted — 35% of registered households are actively re-checking monthly, which is the retention signal that matters more than raw signups for a trust-verification product, since the point of the product is repeated use at each purchase decision, not a one-time signup.

Township & income reality check on these numbers: The pilot ward covers roughly 380 households per municipal ward-boundary estimates, so 148 signups represents genuine penetration (~39% of addressable households in that specific micro-area) rather than a vanity number diluted across an unrealistically large denominator — we are reporting the real, narrow base we actually reached, not projecting from a headline settlement-wide population figure that would inflate the apparent traction.

Honest caveat: This is one ward, one settlement, over five months, with a manual (not yet USSD) channel — it validates the demand-side hypothesis (households will register and re-check) but does not yet validate the automated, multi-ward channel this checkpoint's threshold is really testing readiness for. The next milestone (tracked in Checkpoint 18) is converting this manual pilot into the live USSD flow across at least two additional wards.","b2c":{"signups":148,"mau":52}}

priorArtifacts.name: Team Architecture
priorArtifacts.content:
Current team: Jane Founder is currently the sole full-time operator (consistent with the single-founder ownership structure disclosed in Checkpoint 8), covering vendor relationships, fieldwork, and the manual pilot operations described in Checkpoint 11. This is an honest single-founder team at this stage, not a team dressed up to look larger than it is.

Skills present: Township-based field operations and vendor-network management (three years, prior fintech distribution role, Checkpoint 7), direct customer research capability (household and vendor fieldwork conducted personally across Checkpoints 1, 2, 9), and early-stage fundraising/documentation ability (this submission itself).

Gaps, named specifically rather than glossed over: (1) No technical co-founder or engineer — the USSD system described in Checkpoint 4 does not yet exist as working software; it has been scoped but not built, and this is the single largest execution risk to the venture. (2) No public-health or water-quality technical advisor yet formally engaged, though in early conversation (referenced in Checkpoint 7). (3) No finance/operations hire, currently acceptable given the small pilot scale but a near-term need once vendor count grows past roughly 30-40 (the point at which manual reconciliation of test-strip distribution and vendor payments becomes unmanageable for one person, based on comparable informal-distribution ratios the founder observed in the prior fintech role).

Near-term plan to close the largest gap: The technical co-founder/first engineering hire is the top priority for the next quarter, targeted through South African developer networks (e.g., OfferZen, or direct referral from the founder's existing fintech network) rather than an offshore hire, specifically because the USSD integration requires working knowledge of South African telco short-code and USSD gateway providers (e.g., Clickatell, Africa's Talking), which is a local, not generic, technical skill.

Advisory: One informal advisor relationship exists — a former manager from the founder's prior fintech role, providing guidance on vendor-network economics, unpaid and informal at this stage (no equity or formal advisor agreement yet, disclosed honestly rather than presented as a formal advisory board that does not exist).

We are not recruiting a large team prematurely; the plan is deliberately sequenced — technical hire first, then an operations hire once vendor count justifies it, then a formal advisory board once there is a product to advise on, rather than assembling advisors and headcount ahead of proof that the model works.

priorArtifacts.name: Regulatory & Data Compliance
priorArtifacts.content:
POPIA compliance: Building on the beneficial ownership and entity status disclosed in Checkpoint 8, our data model is designed for POPIA minimisation from the outset. The USSD registration flow (Checkpoint 4/11) collects only: phone number, settlement/ward area, and test-result history — explicitly not ID numbers, home addresses, or names, since none of these are required for the core trust-verification function. Consent is captured as an explicit USSD confirmation step at registration ("Reply YES to receive vendor safety alerts"), logged with a timestamp, satisfying POPIA's requirement for a documented lawful basis (consent) rather than relying on an implied-consent argument. A data retention policy (draft) specifies test-result logs older than 12 months are purged rather than retained indefinitely, and a POPIA-compliant privacy notice (in isiXhosa and English, given the primary pilot ward's language profile) is read out via USSD text at registration rather than assuming households will read an emailed policy document they are unlikely to receive or open.

Tax registration: A SARS (South African Revenue Service) income tax reference number will be obtained automatically upon CIPC company registration completing (per Checkpoint 8's registration-in-progress status); VAT registration is not yet required as projected first-year revenue (modelled in Checkpoint 15) falls below the compulsory VAT registration threshold, and voluntary VAT registration is deliberately deferred until revenue is closer to that threshold, to avoid unnecessary compliance overhead at pre-revenue stage.

Sector-specific compliance: Water quality testing sits adjacent to, but is distinct from, formal municipal water supply regulation (the Blue Drop/Green Drop framework applies to municipal and water-service-authority supply, not informal vendor resale, per our review of the Department of Water and Sanitation's published Blue Drop scope documents) — meaning there is no existing formal licensing regime this venture is required to register under for testing informal vendor water, though we are seeking informal confirmation of this reading from the NGO partner referenced in Checkpoint 10 before finalising, rather than assuming a regulatory gap without verifying it.

B-BBEE: As noted in Checkpoint 5, B-BBEE Level 1-2 contributor status will be pursued once turnover crosses the threshold requiring formal verification (Exempt Micro-Enterprise status applies below that threshold, requiring only a sworn affidavit rather than a full verification audit), which is the compliant approach for a company at this revenue stage rather than paying for premature formal B-BBEE verification.

Honest gap: The consent-language localisation (isiXhosa USSD text) is drafted but not yet tested with actual users for comprehension — this is flagged as a pre-launch validation task, not assumed to be correct simply because it has been translated.

priorArtifacts.name: Unit Economics v1
priorArtifacts.content:
Revenue model: Vendors pay a flat monthly subscription (R40/month) for the verification service — test strips, USSD registration, and the physical trust tag — rather than us taking a cut of their water sales, which our fieldwork (Checkpoint 2) showed vendors would resist given already-thin per-container margins. Households pay nothing directly; the vendor's ability to charge the 10-20% premium (Checkpoint 2) funds their subscription.

CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost, vendor-side): Based on the pilot (Checkpoint 11), vendor onboarding cost is almost entirely founder field-operations time (relationship-building visits, training on the test-strip/USSD process) rather than paid marketing — estimated at R180 per vendor onboarded (roughly 3 hours of founder time at a loaded cost of R60/hour, consistent with early-stage founder opportunity-cost benchmarking used in South African seed-stage models, plus R0 in paid acquisition spend since all 6 pilot vendors came from direct outreach, not ads). This stays low specifically because we are not building or supporting a smartphone app — there is no app-store cost, no device compatibility support burden, and no data-cost subsidy needed, which keeps the onboarding motion cheap and matches the device-class reality from Checkpoint 2.

Household-side CAC is effectively zero: households self-register via USSD after seeing a vendor's tag, so acquisition is vendor-driven, not a separate paid funnel — this is a deliberate structural choice, not an assumption.

COGS (per vendor, monthly): Test strips at approximately R3 each, weekly testing cadence = 4 strips/month = R12. Physical tag replacement (laminated card) amortised at roughly R2/month. Total COGS: R14/vendor/month. Critically, none of this COGS depends on vendor electricity access, so load-shedding (Checkpoint 5) does not increase our cost base the way a powered-equipment-based testing solution would.

Gross margin: R40 revenue - R14 COGS = R26/vendor/month, a 65% gross margin.

Contribution margin: Variable costs beyond COGS include strip/tag distribution logistics (estimated R4/vendor/month for a founder or eventual field agent to restock, based on comparable per-stop informal-distribution logistics costs) and USSD gateway per-transaction fees (approximately R0.50 per check, averaging 8 checks/vendor/month from associated household activity = R4/month). Contribution margin: R26 - R4 - R4 = R18/vendor/month, a 45% contribution margin.

LTV: Assuming an 18-month average vendor retention (conservative estimate pending real churn data, since the pilot is only 5 months old — we are not claiming validated churn we don't have), LTV = R18 x 18 = R324/vendor. Against a R180 CAC, this is an LTV:CAC ratio of approximately 1.8:1 — workable but not yet a strong ratio, and honestly the weakest number in this unit-economics picture; improving vendor retention and/or reducing CAC through referral-driven onboarding (vendors recruiting other vendors, which two of our six pilot vendors have already done organically) is the clearest lever, and is the explicit next-quarter focus rather than a glossed-over weakness.
