This expanded sample found average annual spend on electrical/plumbing/appliance callouts of R2,350/household/year (95% CI roughly R2,050-R2,650), consistent with the original 40-household estimate of R2,500 and now backed by a 3x larger, partially receipt-verified sample. That gives a TAM of roughly R12.9 billion/year in trade spend nationally.

SAM (Serviceable Addressable Market): Restricting to Gauteng metro townships (Soweto, Tembisa, Alexandra, and similar) — roughly 850,000 households (City of Johannesburg and Ekurhuleni municipal household estimates, 2023) — gives a SAM of approximately R2.0 billion/year (using the revised R2,350 figure).

SOM (Serviceable Obtainable Market, Year 1-2), built bottom-up with unit economics reconciled to CP2: Average job value is R2,350/year divided across 3 jobs = approximately R783/job. Applying the 12% commission rate (mid-point of the 10-15% range from the expanded 22-tradesperson interview round, up from the original 9, conducted May-June 2024) gives a platform take of approximately R94/job. Targeting a network of 175 verified tradespeople by month 24, each closing an average of 2.5 jobs/month: 175 x 2.5 x R94 = R41,125/month, or approximately R493,500/year in platform revenue at full Year 2 run-rate. As a share of the R2.0 billion Gauteng SAM, this SOM represents roughly 0.025% market capture in Year 2.

Assumptions and risk: The largest remaining assumption is that tradespeople will actually pay the 12% commission once real money is involved, not just say yes in an interview — CP11 traction data (pilot with paying tradespeople) is where this gets tested with real transactions. The household spend figure is now backed by a 120-household sample with partial receipt verification, which is a material improvement over the original 40-household self-report, though still a founder-run survey rather than a third-party study.

priorArtifacts.name: Problem Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Problem: Households and small businesses in South African townships and peri-urban areas struggle to find electricians, plumbers, and appliance technicians they can trust. Informal tradespeople (the majority of the market) have no standard way to prove they're qualified, insured, or reliable, so customers rely on word-of-mouth, which fails when they move areas or need someone urgently. Tradespeople, in turn, lose jobs to unverified competitors who undercut on price but do unsafe work, and have no way to build a portable reputation across customers.

Evidence: (1) Stats SA Quarterly Labour Force Survey Q3 2023 shows the informal/skilled-trades sector employs a large share of urban workers without formal registration. (2) National Home Builders Registration Council (NHBRC) reporting on unregistered electrical work linked to house fires in Gauteng townships (2022-2023). (3) Department of Employment and Labour data (2023) on artisan registration gaps relative to demand. (4) Interviews with 14 households in Soweto and Tembisa (founder fieldwork, April 2024) citing "found through a neighbour" as the dominant discovery method, with no way to verify qualifications beforehand. (5) Interviews with 9 informal electricians and plumbers (founder fieldwork, April-May 2024) reporting lost jobs to unlicensed competitors and no mechanism to showcase a track record to new customers. (6) City of Johannesburg small-business survey (2023) on informal trades' access to customers beyond their immediate neighbourhood. (7) South African Institute of Electrical Engineers commentary (2022) on the prevalence of unregistered electrical installations in informal settlements. (8) Eskom safety bulletins (2023) on electrical fire risk from non-compliant wiring. (9) GSMA Mobile Economy Sub-Saharan Africa 2023 report on smartphone/WhatsApp penetration relevant to a booking mechanism. (10) Statistics South Africa General Household Survey 2023 on household spend on home repairs and maintenance.

Customer voice: "I had a plumber quote me R400, do a bad job, and I couldn't even remember his surname to complain" — Tembisa resident, interviewed April 2024. "I'm a qualified electrician but customers always ask their cousin first — I have no way to show them my certificate or my past jobs unless I'm standing in their kitchen" — informal electrician, Soweto, interviewed May 2024.

priorArtifacts.name: South African Reality Fit
priorArtifacts.content:
SA Reality Fit — master document for QuickFix Trades:

Load-shedding & infrastructure: Both the household and tradesperson sides operate through WhatsApp, which queues messages through outages rather than requiring a live session — this is a deliberate design choice given Stage 2-4 load-shedding is routine in Gauteng townships (Eskom schedules, 2023-2024). Our own backend (booking matching logic) runs on cloud infrastructure with its own uptime, independent of the founder's or any household's local power/internet — the founder's own admin dashboard access during outages is managed with a mobile hotspot as backup, similar to the approach validated in other Founda21 ventures' equivalent checkpoints.

Data cost & device class: WhatsApp is zero-rated or heavily discounted on major SA networks, so both households (occasional users) and tradespeople (frequent, all-day users checking for leads) are not deterred by data cost the way a native-app-with-push-notifications model would be. Device-wise, founder fieldwork found 34 of 40 surveyed households and all 9 interviewed tradespeople owned Android smartphones capable of running WhatsApp — no iOS-only or high-spec device dependency in the design.

Township & income realities: The target household segment (R6,000-R25,000/month) cannot absorb a subscription-style monthly fee for occasional (2-4x/year) repair needs, which is why the household side of the platform is free to use — monetisation sits entirely on the tradesperson side (commission + optional listing fee), consistent with how these households already behave (paying per job, not per platform). On the tradesperson side, R4,000-R15,000/month earners are price-sensitive to fixed costs, which is why we default to commission-per-completed-job (variable, tied to actual income) rather than a flat monthly fee as the primary pricing model, with the flat listing fee positioned as an optional upgrade for tradespeople who want guaranteed visibility.

This document is the reference point for local-context claims in every other checkpoint — CP4's solution design, CP11's traction interpretation, and CP16's capital pathway all build on the constraints stated here.

priorArtifacts.name: African Scalability Logic
priorArtifacts.content:
Scalability logic: QuickFix Trades' core mechanism (WhatsApp-based lead matching + verification badge + job-completion track record) is not Johannesburg-specific — it depends on three transferable conditions: (1) high WhatsApp/smartphone penetration among both households and tradespeople, (2) a large informal/semi-formal trades workforce without portable reputation, and (3) urban density sufficient for a tradesperson to serve multiple nearby jobs profitably.

Expansion path within South Africa: After Gauteng (Year 1-2), the next markets are eThekwini/Durban and Cape Town metro townships (Khayelitsha, Delft) — both have comparable WhatsApp penetration and informal trades density per Stats SA data, and existing Founda21-network peer ventures (e.g. water-vendor verification in Khayelitsha) suggest the "verification badge for informal service providers" pattern already has local precedent and household familiarity in the Western Cape specifically.

Expansion path across Africa: The same three conditions (WhatsApp-first, informal trades workforce, urban density) hold in Nairobi, Lagos, and Accra, all of which have GSMA-reported WhatsApp penetration comparable to or higher than South Africa. What does NOT transfer directly: payment rails (M-Pesa dominance in Kenya vs. card/EFT in South Africa means the commission-collection mechanism needs to be rebuilt per market, not copy-pasted), and trade licensing/registration bodies differ by country (NHBRC/PIRB equivalents don't exist identically elsewhere), so the "verification" layer needs local recalibration, not just translation.

Real barriers to expansion: regulatory — operating a marketplace that takes commission on trade services may trigger different licensing requirements in each country; logistical — building a new tradesperson-verification pipeline in each city requires local boots-on-the-ground vetting, which doesn't scale purely through software; and trust — the verification badge only means something once it has a track record in that specific market, so each new city effectively restarts the trust-building curve rather than inheriting reputation from prior markets.

priorArtifacts.name: Founder–Problem Fit
priorArtifacts.content: {"recordingLink":"https://youtu.be/unlisted-thabo-founder-statement-demo","statement":"I grew up in Tembisa in a household where my father was an informal electrician for over 20 years — I watched him lose jobs to unlicensed competitors who undercut him on price, and I watched neighbours get burned (literally, in one case a small kitchen fire) by unsafe wiring from those same unlicensed competitors. After studying industrial engineering and working for three years at a logistics-matching startup in Johannesburg, I kept coming back to the fact that the exact problem I'd solved for trucking (matching supply and demand with verified, trackable participants) was the same unsolved problem in my father's trade.\r\n\r\nI've spent the last five months doing this research myself — the 40 household interviews and 9 tradesperson interviews in CP1/CP2 were conducted personally, on foot, in Soweto and Tembisa, not outsourced to a research firm. I'm not building this because I read a trend report; I'm building it because I've seen what happens when trust and reputation don't transfer between jobs for people like my father, and I think a WhatsApp-based verification and matching layer is the most realistic near-term fix given what I know about how these communities actually communicate and pay for things."}

priorArtifacts.name: Customer Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Primary customer segment (demand side): Households and small landlords in Soweto, Tembisa, and similar Gauteng townships, earning R6,000-R25,000/month, who need home repairs (electrical, plumbing, appliance) 2-4 times a year and currently source tradespeople through word-of-mouth or Facebook community groups. They own smartphones and use WhatsApp daily (fieldwork: 34 of 40 households surveyed, April 2024, owned an Android smartphone with active WhatsApp).

Primary customer segment (supply side): Informal and semi-formal electricians, plumbers, and appliance technicians, typically working solo or in pairs, earning R4,000-R15,000/month, who rely entirely on referrals and have no digital presence. Most have basic trade training (apprenticeship or informal mentorship) but few hold full NHBRC/PIRB registration due to cost and paperwork barriers.

Device and connectivity reality: Both sides are smartphone-and-WhatsApp-first, not app-store-first — tradespeople in particular are wary of apps requiring data-heavy downloads or subscriptions. A WhatsApp-based booking and verification flow (business API) is more realistic than requiring a native app install for the tradesperson side in year one.

Willingness to pay: Interviews with 9 tradespeople (April-May 2024) indicate willingness to pay a small monthly listing fee (R50-R150) or a per-job referral commission (10-15%) in exchange for verified leads, since their current customer-acquisition cost is effectively zero but so is their reach beyond their existing network.

priorArtifacts.name: Solution Hypothesis
priorArtifacts.content:
Solution: QuickFix Trades is a WhatsApp-first booking and verification platform connecting households to vetted informal/semi-formal tradespeople. Households message a WhatsApp Business number describing their job (e.g. "geyser leaking"), and are matched with 2-3 verified nearby tradespeople who can respond with availability and an estimated callout fee. Each tradesperson profile carries a verification badge (ID check, trade-skill screening call, and — where held — NHBRC/PIRB registration number) plus a job-completion track record built up on the platform itself, solving the "no portable reputation" problem from CP1.

Why this addresses the CP1 problem directly: households get a way to filter for verified, rated tradespeople instead of relying purely on word-of-mouth (addressing the trust gap), and tradespeople get a channel to reach customers beyond their existing referral network and to build a reputation that follows them job to job (addressing the "no portable reputation, lost jobs to unlicensed competitors" problem).

Load-shedding & infrastructure fit: The WhatsApp-based flow (rather than a data-heavy native app) is deliberately chosen because it works on 3G/patchy connectivity and doesn't require the tradesperson to keep an app running in the background, which matters given intermittent power affecting home WiFi/routers during outages — WhatsApp messages queue and deliver once connectivity returns, unlike a live in-app chat that could time out mid-conversation.

Data cost & device class fit: WhatsApp is typically zero-rated or heavily discounted by SA mobile networks relative to general data, which matters for both the household side (occasional user) and the tradesperson side (would otherwise need to keep a data-hungry app open all day to catch new leads).

label: Thandeka Founder CP4 a1
artifactContent:
GridSense is a lightweight app + SMS fallback that combines Eskom's official stage schedule with real-time, street-level crowdsourced confirmations — users tap a single "power on/power off" button when their own power changes state, and we use that signal to correct the suburb-level official schedule down to street-level accuracy for everyone nearby. This directly solves CP1's core problem: business owners currently can't trust the suburb-level 2-hour-block predictions for their specific street, so they either burn diesel all day defensively or get caught without warning.

Step by step: (1) we ingest Eskom's published stage schedule as a baseline, (2) we layer in crowdsourced on/off taps from GridSense users in the same 500m grid cell, (3) once 3+ users in a cell confirm a state change, we push a corrected prediction to everyone else in that cell via app notification and SMS, (4) our recommendation engine then tells the business owner exactly when to run the fridge/freezer versus switch to battery-conserve mode, based on the corrected outage window — this is the second half of the value: not just "when will power go" but "what should I do about it right now."

Load-shedding/infrastructure fit: the crowdsourcing mechanism specifically compensates for the exact gap identified in CP1 (official schedules deviating 30-90 minutes in townships) — it gets more accurate precisely where the official data is worst, because that's where the most GridSense users are reporting.

Data cost/device fit: the on/off tap is a single button press (near-zero data), predictions are pushed via lightweight push notification or SMS (not a live dashboard the user has to keep open and re-load), and the whole app is under 8MB to install — deliberately built for a 16-32GB entry-level Android device with a R50-R150/month data budget, matching CP2's customer reality exactly.

priorArtifacts.name: Problem Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Small business owners in South African townships — spaza shop owners, hair salons, small manufacturers — lose real money every month because they can't predict exactly when load-shedding will hit their specific street, so they either run diesel generators all day just in case, or get caught without power exactly when a fridge full of stock is at risk.

Eskom's published stage schedules only give suburb-level, roughly 2-hour blocks — not a reliable start/end time for a specific street — and the active stage can change with little notice, so business owners are constantly guessing.

Documented sources (10+):
1. Stats SA (2023) Quarterly Labour Force Survey — approx. 2.3 million township-based informal/small enterprises nationally.
2. Eskom (2024) national load-shedding schedule publication — suburb-block granularity, not street-level.
3. CSIR Energy Centre (2023) report on SME economic losses from load-shedding — R2,000-R10,000/month average for stock-dependent small businesses.
4. World Bank (2023) South Africa Economic Update — load-shedding cited as the top constraint on small business growth.
5. Stellenbosch Business School (2023) survey of 500 township SMEs on load-shedding coping costs.
6. BusinessTech (2024) article on generator diesel cost inflation squeezing small business margins.
7. GridWatch SA (2024) community-reported schedule-accuracy tracking — official predictions deviate 30-90 minutes in township areas regularly.
8. Small Business Institute SA (2023) report on informal sector vulnerability to infrastructure shocks.
9. EskomSePush app store reviews (2024) — aggregated complaints about inaccurate suburb-level predictions specifically in township areas.
10. National Treasury (2023) Budget Review — notes load-shedding's disproportionate impact on informal/township economies.

Customer voice (direct):
- "I lost R3,400 in spoiled airtime and cold drinks stock last month because the schedule said Stage 2 would end at 4pm and it didn't come back until almost 7." — Nomsa, spaza shop owner, Diepsloot (interview, March 2024).
- "I run my generator from 6am just in case, even on days there's no load-shedding at all, because I can't trust the app timing for my exact street." — Sipho, hair salon owner, Soweto (interview, March 2024).
- "My biggest cost isn't the diesel, it's guessing wrong and losing a full day's fridge stock twice a month." — Thabo, spaza owner, Khayelitsha (WhatsApp voice note transcript, April 2024).

priorArtifacts.name: Customer Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Our customer is a township small business owner in Gauteng and Western Cape — spaza shop owners, hair salon owners, and small manufacturers — typically aged 28-55, with roughly 55% of our current pilot customers being women-owned businesses. They run a single-room or small storefront in areas like Soweto, Diepsloot, Khayelitsha, or Delft, and net R8,000-R25,000/month, most of it reinvested into stock or equipment.

Device and data reality: they carry an entry-level Android smartphone (typically an Itel or Mobicel under R2,500, 16-32GB storage) often shared with family, with a data budget of R50-R150/month spent mostly on WhatsApp. They are wary of downloading large apps or apps that eat data in the background — this directly shapes our product decision to lead with a lightweight app plus an SMS fallback channel, not a data-heavy dashboard.

They currently rely on EskomSePush (when they have spare data) or township WhatsApp groups for load-shedding info, and either own or rent a small 2.5-5kVA generator, spending R800-R2,500/month on diesel during high-stage periods — this is the exact budget line GridSense reduces.

Township and income realities: our pricing (R149/month) is deliberately benchmarked against what they already spend guessing wrong on diesel and spoiled stock in a single bad week, not against a Silicon Valley SaaS price point — verified against the R2,000-R10,000/month loss figures from CP1's CSIR source and confirmed directly with 3 pilot customers during onboarding interviews in March 2024.

priorArtifacts.name: Market Sizing (Africa-calibrated)
priorArtifacts.content:
TAM (Africa-calibrated, not US/EU benchmarks): ~15 million power-insecure small businesses across Sub-Saharan Africa's four largest informal-SME economies (South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana) facing chronic grid instability, per AfDB (2023) Africa Energy Outlook electricity-access data. This uses actual regional business-density and grid-reliability figures, not a top-down "% of US SaaS TAM" guess.

SAM: South African township/informal SMEs specifically affected by Eskom's scheduled (not just unreliable) load-shedding — our core product depends on structured stage-schedule data, which only exists in the SA market today. Of the 2.3 million township-based enterprises (Stats SA 2023, cited in CP1), roughly 20% carry power-dependent stock or equipment (fridges, freezers, hair equipment, small manufacturing tools) per the CSIR (2023) SME loss study cross-referenced against Stats SA's informal-sector equipment-ownership breakdown. Maths: 2,300,000 x 0.20 = 460,000 SAM.

SOM (Year 1, Gauteng + Western Cape only): reachable via direct spaza-shop-association and township-trader-forum partnerships. National Spaza Shop Association's Gauteng chapter lists ~8,000 active members; Western Cape Informal Traders Forum lists ~5,000. At a 60% realistic conversion rate for association-referred leads (benchmarked against comparable township fintech-onboarding case studies, e.g. Yoco's early merchant-association rollout), that's (8,000 + 5,000) x 0.60 = 7,800, rounded to a conservative 7,500 addressable in year 1 given our current 2-person team's onboarding capacity.

This SOM is achievable specifically because it rides on existing association trust networks rather than cold outreach — our 3 current pilots came through exactly this channel.

label: Thandeka Founder CP6 a1
artifactContent:
After establishing GridSense in Gauteng and Western Cape, our next markets are Lagos, Nigeria and Nairobi, Kenya — both have well-documented grid instability affecting informal/township-equivalent SMEs, which is the precondition for our model to matter.

What changes: (1) Data baseline — Nigeria's DisCos publish far less structured outage schedules than Eskom's stage system, so our Nigeria model runs almost entirely on crowdsourced signal with no official baseline to correct, requiring a higher initial density of users per grid cell before predictions activate. Kenya's outages are more fault-driven than scheduled, so the same applies there. (2) Payment rails — Kenya's dominant channel is M-Pesa, not bank debit order like our SA billing; Nigeria needs both bank transfer and USSD-based payment support. (3) Distribution channel — Nigeria's market-trader associations and Kenya's chama/table-banking groups replace SA's spaza-shop associations as the trust-building entry point; the mechanism (partner with an existing trusted local network) stays the same, the specific network changes. (4) Language — Nigerian Pidgin/Yoruba/Hausa and Swahili localisation for SMS and app copy.

What stays the same: the core crowdsourced correction algorithm, the smart backup-power recommendation engine, the under-8MB lightweight app design for low-end devices and small data budgets, and the association-partnership go-to-market model — only the specific partner network changes per country, not the approach itself.

Real barriers: regulatory (each country needs its own local SMS-gateway/telco partnership and, in Nigeria's case, NDPR data-protection registration before launch); logistical (each new market needs an on-the-ground community manager to seed the first 3+ crowdsourced reporters per grid cell before the correction layer has any value — this is a slower, more manual cold-start than SA where Eskom's baseline schedule already gives us something useful on day one); cultural (each market's trust network takes real relationship-building time to access, not just a translated pitch deck); infrastructural (Kenya's fault-driven outage pattern means our model there needs a materially higher crowdsourced-user density before it's useful, since there's no official schedule to correct against at all — this is the single biggest expansion risk and the reason Kenya is planned after Nigeria, not simultaneously).

priorArtifacts.name: South African Reality Fit
priorArtifacts.content:
This is GridSense's master SA Reality Fit document — every later checkpoint (unit economics, financial model, capital pathway, roadmap) builds on the three local-context facts established here.

Load-shedding & infrastructure: South Africa runs on a stage-based national load-shedding system (Stage 1-8, Eskom 2024) where higher stages mean more frequent, longer outages, but the published suburb-block schedule deviates 30-90 minutes from reality in townships specifically (GridSense SA 2024 tracking, cited in CP1) because infrastructure age and localised faults aren't reflected in the national schedule. Our product design assumes intermittent, unpredictable connectivity for both the business owner's phone and any backend sync — the app must function fully offline between syncs and queue outbound SMS/data when the network itself drops during outages, which we've built as a core requirement, not an afterthought.

Data cost & device class: our real customers (CP2) run entry-level Android devices (16-32GB storage, R2,500 or under) on R50-R150/month data budgets, dominated by WhatsApp usage. This rules out any product design that assumes always-on connectivity, large background sync, or a heavy native app — GridSense is under 8MB installed and every user action (the on/off tap) costs less data than a single WhatsApp text message.

priorArtifacts.name: Solution Hypothesis
priorArtifacts.content:
GridSense is a lightweight app + SMS fallback that combines Eskom's official stage schedule with real-time, street-level crowdsourced confirmations — users tap a single "power on/power off" button when their own power changes state, and we use that signal to correct the suburb-level official schedule down to street-level accuracy for everyone nearby. This directly solves CP1's core problem: business owners currently can't trust the suburb-level 2-hour-block predictions for their specific street, so they either burn diesel all day defensively or get caught without warning.

Step by step: (1) we ingest Eskom's published stage schedule as a baseline, (2) we layer in crowdsourced on/off taps from GridSense users in the same 500m grid cell, (3) once 3+ users in a cell confirm a state change, we push a corrected prediction to everyone else in that cell via app notification and SMS, (4) our recommendation engine then tells the business owner exactly when to run the fridge/freezer versus switch to battery-conserve mode, based on the corrected outage window.

Early validation: during our March-April 2024 pilot with 3 Soweto/Diepsloot businesses, the crowdsourced correction layer flagged 11 of 14 load-shedding events at least 20 minutes earlier or later than Eskom's official block predicted, matching what actually happened on the ground in 9 of those 11 cases (verified by comparing app timestamps against pilot users' own generator start/stop logs) — early but real evidence that the correction mechanism works, not just a theoretical claim.

Load-shedding/infrastructure fit: the crowdsourcing mechanism specifically compensates for the exact gap identified in CP1 (official schedules deviating 30-90 minutes in townships) — it gets more accurate precisely where the official data is worst, because that's where the most GridSense users are reporting.

Data cost/device fit: the on/off tap is a single button press (near-zero data), predictions are pushed via lightweight push notification or SMS (not a live dashboard the user has to keep open and re-load), and the whole app is under 8MB to install — deliberately built for a 16-32GB entry-level Android device with a R50-R150/month data budget, matching CP2's customer reality exactly.

priorArtifacts.name: Customer Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Our customer is a township small business owner in Gauteng and Western Cape — spaza shop owners, hair salon owners, and small manufacturers — typically aged 28-55, with roughly 55% of our current pilot customers being women-owned businesses. They run a single-room or small storefront in areas like Soweto, Diepsloot, Khayelitsha, or Delft, and net R8,000-R25,000/month, most of it reinvested into stock or equipment.

Device and data reality: they carry an entry-level Android smartphone (typically an Itel or Mobicel under R2,500, 16-32GB storage) often shared with family, with a data budget of R50-R150/month spent mostly on WhatsApp. They are wary of downloading large apps or apps that eat data in the background — this directly shapes our product decision to lead with a lightweight app plus an SMS fallback channel, not a data-heavy dashboard.

They currently rely on EskomSePush (when they have spare data) or township WhatsApp groups for load-shedding info, and either own or rent a small 2.5-5kVA generator, spending R800-R2,500/month on diesel during high-stage periods — this is the exact budget line GridSense reduces.

Township and income realities: our pricing (R149/month) is deliberately benchmarked against what they already spend guessing wrong on diesel and spoiled stock in a single bad week, not against a Silicon Valley SaaS price point — verified against the R2,000-R10,000/month loss figures from CP1's CSIR source and confirmed directly with 3 pilot customers during onboarding interviews in March 2024.

priorArtifacts.content:
TAM (Africa-calibrated, not US/EU benchmarks): ~15 million power-insecure small businesses across Sub-Saharan Africa's four largest informal-SME economies (South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana) facing chronic grid instability, per AfDB (2023) Africa Energy Outlook electricity-access data. This uses actual regional business-density and grid-reliability figures, not a top-down "% of US SaaS TAM" guess.

SAM: South African township/informal SMEs specifically affected by Eskom's scheduled (not just unreliable) load-shedding — our core product depends on structured stage-schedule data, which only exists in the SA market today. Of the 2.3 million township-based enterprises (Stats SA 2023, cited in CP1), roughly 20% carry power-dependent stock or equipment (fridges, freezers, hair equipment, small manufacturing tools) per the CSIR (2023) SME loss study cross-referenced against Stats SA's informal-sector equipment-ownership breakdown. Maths: 2,300,000 x 0.20 = 460,000 SAM.

SOM (Year 1, Gauteng + Western Cape only): reachable via direct spaza-shop-association and township-trader-forum partnerships. National Spaza Shop Association's Gauteng chapter lists ~8,000 active members; Western Cape Informal Traders Forum lists ~5,000. At a 60% realistic conversion rate for association-referred leads (benchmarked against comparable township fintech-onboarding case studies, e.g. Yoco's early merchant-association rollout), that's (8,000 + 5,000) x 0.60 = 7,800, rounded to a conservative 7,500 addressable in year 1 given our current 2-person team's onboarding capacity.

This SOM is achievable specifically because it rides on existing association trust networks rather than cold outreach — our 3 current pilots came through exactly this channel.

priorArtifacts.name: South African Reality Fit
priorArtifacts.content:
This is GridSense's master SA Reality Fit document — every later checkpoint (unit economics, financial model, capital pathway, roadmap) builds on the three local-context facts established here.

Load-shedding & infrastructure: South Africa runs on a stage-based national load-shedding system (Stage 1-8, Eskom 2024) where higher stages mean more frequent, longer outages, but the published suburb-block schedule deviates 30-90 minutes from reality in townships specifically (GridSense SA 2024 tracking, cited in CP1) because infrastructure age and localised faults aren't reflected in the national schedule. Our product design assumes intermittent, unpredictable connectivity for both the business owner's phone and any backend sync — the app must function fully offline between syncs and queue outbound SMS/data when the network itself drops during outages, which we've built as a core requirement, not an afterthought.

Data cost & device class: our real customers (CP2) run entry-level Android devices (16-32GB storage, R2,500 or under) on R50-R150/month data budgets, dominated by WhatsApp usage. This rules out any product design that assumes always-on connectivity, large background sync, or a heavy native app — GridSense is under 8MB installed and every user action (the on/off tap) costs less data than a single WhatsApp text message.

Township & income realities: our customers net R8,000-R25,000/month and currently lose R2,000-R10,000/month (CSIR 2023, cited in CP1) to diesel waste and stock spoilage from unpredictable load-shedding — this is the exact ceiling our R149/month price point must sit comfortably under to be adopted, and the exact reason our go-to-market (CP16) leans on trusted spaza-association channels rather than paid digital acquisition, which this customer segment doesn't respond to at any meaningful rate based on our 3 pilots' feedback.

priorArtifacts.name: African Scalability Logic
priorArtifacts.content:
After establishing GridSense in Gauteng and Western Cape, our next markets are Lagos, Nigeria and Nairobi, Kenya — both have well-documented grid instability affecting informal/township-equivalent SMEs, which is the precondition for our model to matter.

What changes: (1) Data baseline — Nigeria's DisCos publish far less structured outage schedules than Eskom's stage system, so our Nigeria model runs almost entirely on crowdsourced signal with no official baseline to correct, requiring a higher initial density of users per grid cell before predictions activate. Kenya's outages are more fault-driven than scheduled, so the same applies there. (2) Payment rails — Kenya's dominant channel is M-Pesa, not bank debit order like our SA billing; Nigeria needs both bank transfer and USSD-based payment support. (3) Distribution channel — Nigeria's market-trader associations and Kenya's chama/table-banking groups replace SA's spaza-shop associations as the trust-building entry point; the mechanism (partner with an existing trusted local network) stays the same, the specific network changes. (4) Language — Nigerian Pidgin/Yoruba/Hausa and Swahili localisation for SMS and app copy.

What stays the same: the core crowdsourced correction algorithm, the smart backup-power recommendation engine, the under-8MB lightweight app design for low-end devices and small data budgets, and the association-partnership go-to-market model — only the specific partner network changes per country, not the approach itself.

Real barriers: regulatory (each country needs its own local SMS-gateway/telco partnership and, in Nigeria's case, NDPR data-protection registration before launch); logistical (each new market needs an on-the-ground community manager to seed the first 3+ crowdsourced reporters per grid cell before the correction layer has any value — this is a slower, more manual cold-start than SA where Eskom's baseline schedule already gives us something useful on day one); cultural (each market's trust network takes real relationship-building time to access, not just a translated pitch deck); infrastructural (Kenya's fault-driven outage pattern means our model there needs a materially higher crowdsourced-user density before it's useful, since there's no official schedule to correct against at all — this is the single biggest expansion risk and the reason Kenya is planned after Nigeria, not simultaneously).

priorArtifacts.name: Brand & Positioning
priorArtifacts.content:
Name: GridSense — deliberately plain English ("grid" for the power grid, "sense" for intelligent prediction), chosen because it needs to be said over the phone, in a WhatsApp voice note, or via word-of-mouth referral between spaza shop owners without translation ambiguity across the isiZulu/Sesotho/English mix common in our target townships.

Identity: positioned as a practical, no-nonsense tool for business owners, not a consumer lifestyle app — our visual identity uses a single traffic-light-style colour code (green/amber/red) for power status, deliberately matching the literacy-accessibility guidance used in SA public-health communication campaigns rather than a logo-dependent brand mark, because the trust signal that matters is instant legibility at a glance, not visual polish.

Positioning statement: "The app that knows your street's power schedule better than Eskom does." This is a specific, falsifiable claim (not "smart energy for a smarter future") and it's exactly what our pilot data (CP4) supports — 9 of 11 crowdsourced corrections matched reality where the official schedule didn't.

Defensibility against a copycat: our real moat is the crowdsourced data density itself, not the app or the algorithm, which a competitor could rebuild in weeks. A new entrant starting with zero users has zero correction accuracy — they'd need to first build the same density of trusted, active reporters per grid cell that we're building today through spaza-association partnerships, which took real relationship time to access, not just capital. This is a data-network-effect moat, not a feature moat, and it compounds the longer we operate before a copycat starts.

Contribution margin (65%): gross margin minus amortized CAC over an assumed 12-month payback window (R450/12 = R37.50/month) and basic support cost (~R10/month/user). (149-33-37.50-10)/149 ≈ 65%.

Honest caveat: LTV:CAC of 2682:450 (~6:1) looks strong but rests on an unproven 18-month retention assumption with only 2 months of real paying-customer data — the real test comes once our first cohort crosses 6 and 12 months."}

priorArtifacts.name: Business Model & Financial Projections
priorArtifacts.content:
[Uploaded file: gridsense-financial-model.pdf, stored at cmrdi6zsw0000sou4fxsryq8u/checkpoint-15/attempt-1.pdf]

3-statement model summary (full model attached above, 24-month bottom-up build):

Income statement build: starting from our SOM of 7,500 reachable Gauteng/Western Cape businesses (CP3), we assume a conservative 12% penetration by month 24 (900 paying businesses) — bottom-up from our actual pilot conversion rate of 2/3 (67%) applied against a realistic association-outreach pace of 40-60 new signups/month once our CP16-funded partnerships hire is in place, not a top-down "capture 1% of TAM" guess. At R149/month ARPU, that's R134,100 MRR by month 24.

Cost build: direct costs per CP14 (SMS gateway ~R8/user/month, hosting ~R25/user/month) scale linearly with users; team costs step up in month 3 (technical co-founder hire, ~R35,000/month) and month 6 (partnerships hire, ~R28,000/month), funded by the CP16 raise.

Balance sheet: main assets are cash from the raise and accrued receivables (customers billed monthly in advance via debit order, so receivables stay near-zero); main liability is the CP16 grant/equity funding itself, held as cash until deployed against the milestone schedule in CP18.

Cash flow: burns approximately R95,000/month in months 1-6 (team ramp before revenue catches up), breaks even on a monthly cash basis around month 16 at our base-case penetration curve, giving roughly 18 months of runway on the R650,000 CP16 raise before needing a follow-on round.

Load-shedding/infrastructure cost line: we've explicitly budgeted R3,500/month for backup power and connectivity redundancy for our own small ops team, since our own operations are exposed to the same grid instability our customers face — this is a real, budgeted line item, not an oversight.

Every assumption above (penetration rate, ARPU, cost-per-user, hiring timeline) is stated with its source, per the requirement — the base case is deliberately conservative relative to our SOM ceiling from CP3, not an optimistic hockey-stick.

priorArtifacts.name: Capital Pathway
priorArtifacts.content:
We're raising R650,000, structured as a blend: R400,000 as an ESD/impact grant (targeting corporate ESD programmes and DFI-adjacent impact funds, given our majority Black-women-owned status and township-focused impact thesis) plus R250,000 as convertible equity from an angel or early-stage impact fund, rather than a single clean equity round — this reflects the reality that a pre-revenue-adjacent township SaaS venture at our stage has genuine access to South African grant capital that a pure-equity story would leave on the table.

Milestone-tied use of funds: R245,000 (month 0-6) funds a full-time technical co-founder or senior engineer hire, directly addressing the CP12 team gap and enabling us to build the automated crowdsource-density onboarding flow that currently requires manual community-manager effort. R196,000 (month 3-9) funds a dedicated partnerships/sales hire to scale past the 40-60 signups/month our founder can personally manage today, targeting the 900-paying-business milestone from CP15's base case. R119,000 (month 1-12) covers the direct cost-per-user scaling (SMS gateway, hosting) as we grow from 2 to roughly 300+ paying businesses in year one. R90,000 is held as working-capital buffer against the load-shedding-driven cost volatility flagged in CP15.

SA capital landscape fit: we're specifically targeting corporate ESD programmes with township-SME development mandates (where our beneficiary profile is a direct fit) and DFI-adjacent impact-first funds rather than traditional VC, because traditional VC's return timelines and equity expectations don't match a venture whose moat (CP9) is data-network density built over years, not a fast-scaling consumer app — we are deliberately not pitching this as a venture-scale outlier to investors who aren't the right fit for this stage and structure.

priorArtifacts.name: Problem Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Small business owners in South African townships — spaza shop owners, hair salons, small manufacturers — lose real money every month because they can't predict exactly when load-shedding will hit their specific street, so they either run diesel generators all day just in case, or get caught without power exactly when a fridge full of stock is at risk.

Eskom's published stage schedules only give suburb-level, roughly 2-hour blocks — not a reliable start/end time for a specific street — and the active stage can change with little notice, so business owners are constantly guessing.

Documented sources (10+):
1. Stats SA (2023) Quarterly Labour Force Survey — approx. 2.3 million township-based informal/small enterprises nationally.
2. Eskom (2024) national load-shedding schedule publication — suburb-block granularity, not street-level.
3. CSIR Energy Centre (2023) report on SME economic losses from load-shedding — R2,000-R10,000/month average for stock-dependent small businesses.
4. World Bank (2023) South Africa Economic Update — load-shedding cited as the top constraint on small business growth.
5. Stellenbosch Business School (2023) survey of 500 township SMEs on load-shedding coping costs.
6. BusinessTech (2024) article on generator diesel cost inflation squeezing small business margins.
7. GridWatch SA (2024) community-reported schedule-accuracy tracking — official predictions deviate 30-90 minutes in township areas regularly.
8. Small Business Institute SA (2023) report on informal sector vulnerability to infrastructure shocks.
9. EskomSePush app store reviews (2024) — aggregated complaints about inaccurate suburb-level predictions specifically in township areas.
10. National Treasury (2023) Budget Review — notes load-shedding's disproportionate impact on informal/township economies.

Customer voice (direct):
- "I lost R3,400 in spoiled airtime and cold drinks stock last month because the schedule said Stage 2 would end at 4pm and it didn't come back until almost 7." — Nomsa, spaza shop owner, Diepsloot (interview, March 2024).
- "I run my generator from 6am just in case, even on days there's no load-shedding at all, because I can't trust the app timing for my exact street." — Sipho, hair salon owner, Soweto (interview, March 2024).
- "My biggest cost isn't the diesel, it's guessing wrong and losing a full day's fridge stock twice a month." — Thabo, spaza owner, Khayelitsha (WhatsApp voice note transcript, April 2024).

priorArtifacts.name: Moat & Risk Architecture
priorArtifacts.content:
Defensibility: our moat is the crowdsourced-correction data density itself (CP9) — a competitor can copy our app and algorithm in weeks, but they can't copy the density of trusted, active on/off reporters we've built per grid cell without repeating the same slow, relationship-based association partnerships, which took real time to access.

Honest risk catalogue:

Regulatory risk: if Eskom itself materially improves its own schedule granularity to street-level (unlikely near-term given current infrastructure, but possible over 3-5 years with smart-meter rollout), our core correction advantage narrows. Mitigation: our recommendation engine (not just the prediction) becomes the more durable value layer if this happens.

Competitive risk: EskomSePush (the incumbent consumer app) could add a business-tier product with similar crowdsourcing. They have distribution advantage but no township-SME-specific go-to-market relationships today — this is a real threat, not a hypothetical one, and our defense is moving faster into association partnerships than they're incentivised to.

Operational risk: our crowdsourcing model requires a minimum density (3+ active reporters per grid cell) to produce value — in low-density areas or early in a new market, the product simply doesn't work as well, which is a genuine cold-start weakness we haven't fully solved, only partially mitigated by leaning on Eskom's baseline schedule where crowdsourced density is thin.

Key-person risk: with only 2 team members (CP12), losing either Thandeka or Bongani in the next 6 months would materially disrupt both product development and the founder-led sales motion — this is a real and current risk, not a sanitised one, and it's the direct reason CP16's raise prioritises hiring before scaling marketing spend.

Financial risk: our LTV assumption (CP14) rests on an 18-month retention benchmark from a different company's product, not our own measured data — if our actual retention comes in materially lower, the unit economics case weakens meaningfully, and we don't have enough of our own cohort data yet to rule that out.

This is GridSense's master SA Reality Fit document — every later checkpoint (unit economics, financial model, capital pathway, roadmap) builds on the three local-context facts established here.

Load-shedding & infrastructure: South Africa runs on a stage-based national load-shedding system (Stage 1-8, Eskom 2024) where higher stages mean more frequent, longer outages, but the published suburb-block schedule deviates 30-90 minutes from reality in townships specifically (GridSense SA 2024 tracking, cited in CP1) because infrastructure age and localised faults aren't reflected in the national schedule. priorArtifacts.content:
Name: GridSense — deliberately plain English ("grid" for the power grid, "sense" for intelligent prediction), chosen because it needs to be said over the phone, in a WhatsApp voice note, or via word-of-mouth referral between spaza shop owners without translation ambiguity across the isiZulu/Sesotho/English mix common in our target townships.

Identity: positioned as a practical, no-nonsense tool for business owners, not a consumer lifestyle app — our visual identity uses a single traffic-light-style colour code (green/amber/red) for power status, deliberately matching the literacy-accessibility guidance used in SA public-health communication campaigns rather than a logo-dependent brand mark, because the trust signal that matters is instant legibility at a glance, not visual polish.

Positioning statement: "The app that knows your street's power schedule better than Eskom does." This is a specific, falsifiable claim (not "smart energy for a smarter future") and it's exactly what our pilot data (CP4) supports — 9 of 11 crowdsourced corrections matched reality where the official schedule didn't.

Defensibility against a copycat: our real moat is the crowdsourced data density itself, not the app or the algorithm, which a competitor could rebuild in weeks. A new entrant starting with zero users has zero correction accuracy — they'd need to first build the same density of trusted, active reporters per grid cell that we're building today through spaza-association partnerships, which took real relationship time to access, not just capital. This is a data-network-effect moat, not a feature moat, and it compounds the longer we operate before a copycat starts.

priorArtifacts.name: Problem Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Small business owners in South African townships — spaza shop owners, hair salons, small manufacturers — lose real money every month because they can't predict exactly when load-shedding will hit their specific street, so they either run diesel generators all day just in case, or get caught without power exactly when a fridge full of stock is at risk.

Eskom's published stage schedules only give suburb-level, roughly 2-hour blocks — not a reliable start/end time for a specific street — and the active stage can change with little notice, so business owners are constantly guessing.

Documented sources (10+):
1. Stats SA (2023) Quarterly Labour Force Survey — approx. 2.3 million township-based informal/small enterprises nationally.
2. Eskom (2024) national load-shedding schedule publication — suburb-block granularity, not street-level.
3. CSIR Energy Centre (2023) report on SME economic losses from load-shedding — R2,000-R10,000/month average for stock-dependent small businesses.
4. World Bank (2023) South Africa Economic Update — load-shedding cited as the top constraint on small business growth.
5. Stellenbosch Business School (2023) survey of 500 township SMEs on load-shedding coping costs.
6. BusinessTech (2024) article on generator diesel cost inflation squeezing small business margins.
7. GridWatch SA (2024) community-reported schedule-accuracy tracking — official predictions deviate 30-90 minutes in township areas regularly.
8. Small Business Institute SA (2023) report on informal sector vulnerability to infrastructure shocks.
9. EskomSePush app store reviews (2024) — aggregated complaints about inaccurate suburb-level predictions specifically in township areas.
10. National Treasury (2023) Budget Review — notes load-shedding's disproportionate impact on informal/township economies.

Customer voice (direct):
- "I lost R3,400 in spoiled airtime and cold drinks stock last month because the schedule said Stage 2 would end at 4pm and it didn't come back until almost 7." — Nomsa, spaza shop owner, Diepsloot (interview, March 2024).
- "I run my generator from 6am just in case, even on days there's no load-shedding at all, because I can't trust the app timing for my exact street." — Sipho, hair salon owner, Soweto (interview, March 2024).
- "My biggest cost isn't the diesel, it's guessing wrong and losing a full day's fridge stock twice a month." — Thabo, spaza owner, Khayelitsha (WhatsApp voice note transcript, April 2024).

priorArtifacts.name: Moat & Risk Architecture
priorArtifacts.content:
Defensibility: our moat is the crowdsourced-correction data density itself (CP9) — a competitor can copy our app and algorithm in weeks, but they can't copy the density of trusted, active on/off reporters we've built per grid cell without repeating the same slow, relationship-based association partnerships, which took real time to access.

Honest risk catalogue:

Regulatory risk: if Eskom itself materially improves its own schedule granularity to street-level (unlikely near-term given current infrastructure, but possible over 3-5 years with smart-meter rollout), our core correction advantage narrows. Mitigation: our recommendation engine (not just the prediction) becomes the more durable value layer if this happens.

Competitive risk: EskomSePush (the incumbent consumer app) could add a business-tier product with similar crowdsourcing. They have distribution advantage but no township-SME-specific go-to-market relationships today — this is a real threat, not a hypothetical one, and our defense is moving faster into association partnerships than they're incentivised to.

Operational risk: our crowdsourcing model requires a minimum density (3+ active reporters per grid cell) to produce value — in low-density areas or early in a new market, the product simply doesn't work as well, which is a genuine cold-start weakness we haven't fully solved, only partially mitigated by leaning on Eskom's baseline schedule where crowdsourced density is thin.

Key-person risk: with only 2 team members (CP12), losing either Thandeka or Bongani in the next 6 months would materially disrupt both product development and the founder-led sales motion — this is a real and current risk, not a sanitised one, and it's the direct reason CP16's raise prioritises hiring before scaling marketing spend.

Financial risk: our LTV assumption (CP14) rests on an 18-month retention benchmark from a different company's product, not our own measured data — if our actual retention comes in materially lower, the unit economics case weakens meaningfully, and we don't have enough of our own cohort data yet to rule that out.

priorArtifacts.name: Solution Hypothesis
priorArtifacts.content:
GridSense is a lightweight app + SMS fallback that combines Eskom's official stage schedule with real-time, street-level crowdsourced confirmations — users tap a single "power on/power off" button when their own power changes state, and we use that signal to correct the suburb-level official schedule down to street-level accuracy for everyone nearby. This directly solves CP1's core problem: business owners currently can't trust the suburb-level 2-hour-block predictions for their specific street, so they either burn diesel all day defensively or get caught without warning.

Step by step: (1) we ingest Eskom's published stage schedule as a baseline, (2) we layer in crowdsourced on/off taps from GridSense users in the same 500m grid cell, (3) once 3+ users in a cell confirm a state change, we push a corrected prediction to everyone else in that cell via app notification and SMS, (4) our recommendation engine then tells the business owner exactly when to run the fridge/freezer versus switch to battery-conserve mode, based on the corrected outage window.

Early validation: during our March-April 2024 pilot with 3 Soweto/Diepsloot businesses, the crowdsourced correction layer flagged 11 of 14 load-shedding events at least 20 minutes earlier or later than Eskom's official block predicted, matching what actually happened on the ground in 9 of those 11 cases (verified by comparing app timestamps against pilot users' own generator start/stop logs) — early but real evidence that the correction mechanism works, not just a theoretical claim.

Load-shedding/infrastructure fit: the crowdsourcing mechanism specifically compensates for the exact gap identified in CP1 (official schedules deviating 30-90 minutes in townships) — it gets more accurate precisely where the official data is worst, because that's where the most GridSense users are reporting.

Data cost/device fit: the on/off tap is a single button press (near-zero data), predictions are pushed via lightweight push notification or SMS (not a live dashboard the user has to keep open and re-load), and the whole app is under 8MB to install — deliberately built for a 16-32GB entry-level Android device with a R50-R150/month data budget, matching CP2's customer reality exactly.

priorArtifacts.content:
Our customer is a township small business owner in Gauteng and Western Cape — spaza shop owners, hair salon owners, and small manufacturers — typically aged 28-55, with roughly 55% of our current pilot customers being women-owned businesses. They run a single-room or small storefront in areas like Soweto, Diepsloot, Khayelitsha, or Delft, and net R8,000-R25,000/month, most of it reinvested into stock or equipment.

Device and data reality: they carry an entry-level Android smartphone (typically an Itel or Mobicel under R2,500, 16-32GB storage) often shared with family, with a data budget of R50-R150/month spent mostly on WhatsApp. They are wary of downloading large apps or apps that eat data in the background — this directly shapes our product decision to lead with a lightweight app plus an SMS fallback channel, not a data-heavy dashboard.

They currently rely on EskomSePush (when they have spare data) or township WhatsApp groups for load-shedding info, and either own or rent a small 2.5-5kVA generator, spending R800-R2,500/month on diesel during high-stage periods — this is the exact budget line GridSense reduces.

Township and income realities: our pricing (R149/month) is deliberately benchmarked against what they already spend guessing wrong on diesel and spoiled stock in a single bad week, not against a Silicon Valley SaaS price point — verified against the R2,000-R10,000/month loss figures from CP1's CSIR source and confirmed directly with 3 pilot customers during onboarding interviews in March 2024.

priorArtifacts.name: Solution Hypothesis
priorArtifacts.content:
GridSense is a lightweight app + SMS fallback that combines Eskom's official stage schedule with real-time, street-level crowdsourced confirmations — users tap a single "power on/power off" button when their own power changes state, and we use that signal to correct the suburb-level official schedule down to street-level accuracy for everyone nearby. This directly solves CP1's core problem: business owners currently can't trust the suburb-level 2-hour-block predictions for their specific street, so they either burn diesel all day defensively or get caught without warning.

Step by step: (1) we ingest Eskom's published stage schedule as a baseline, (2) we layer in crowdsourced on/off taps from GridSense users in the same 500m grid cell, (3) once 3+ users in a cell confirm a state change, we push a corrected prediction to everyone else in that cell via app notification and SMS, (4) our recommendation engine then tells the business owner exactly when to run the fridge/freezer versus switch to battery-conserve mode, based on the corrected outage window.

Early validation: during our March-April 2024 pilot with 3 Soweto/Diepsloot businesses, the crowdsourced correction layer flagged 11 of 14 load-shedding events at least 20 minutes earlier or later than Eskom's official block predicted, matching what actually happened on the ground in 9 of those 11 cases (verified by comparing app timestamps against pilot users' own generator start/stop logs) — early but real evidence that the correction mechanism works, not just a theoretical claim.

Load-shedding/infrastructure fit: the crowdsourcing mechanism specifically compensates for the exact gap identified in CP1 (official schedules deviating 30-90 minutes in townships) — it gets more accurate precisely where the official data is worst, because that's where the most GridSense users are reporting.

Data cost/device fit: the on/off tap is a single button press (near-zero data), predictions are pushed via lightweight push notification or SMS (not a live dashboard the user has to keep open and re-load), and the whole app is under 8MB to install — deliberately built for a 16-32GB entry-level Android device with a R50-R150/month data budget, matching CP2's customer reality exactly.

TAM (Africa-calibrated, not US/EU benchmarks): ~15 million power-insecure small businesses across Sub-Saharan Africa's four largest informal-SME economies (South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana) facing chronic grid instability, per AfDB (2023) Africa Energy Outlook electricity-access data. SAM: South African township/informal SMEs specifically affected by Eskom's scheduled (not just unreliable) load-shedding — our core product depends on structured stage-schedule data, which only exists in the SA market today. Of the 2.3 million township-based enterprises (Stats SA 2023, cited in CP1), roughly 20% carry power-dependent stock or equipment (fridges, freezers, hair equipment, small manufacturing tools) per the CSIR (2023) SME loss study cross-referenced against Stats SA's informal-sector equipment-ownership breakdown. Maths: 2,300,000 x 0.20 = 460,000 SAM.

SOM (Year 1, Gauteng + Western Cape only): reachable via direct spaza-shop-association and township-trader-forum partnerships. National Spaza Shop Association's Gauteng chapter lists ~8,000 active members; Western Cape Informal Traders Forum lists ~5,000. At a 60% realistic conversion rate for association-referred leads (benchmarked against comparable township fintech-onboarding case studies, e.g. Yoco's early merchant-association rollout), that's (8,000 + 5,000) x 0.60 = 7,800, rounded to a conservative 7,500 addressable in year 1 given our current 2-person team's onboarding capacity.

This SOM is achievable specifically because it rides on existing association trust networks rather than cold outreach — our 3 current pilots came through exactly this channel.

priorArtifacts.name: South African Reality Fit
priorArtifacts.content:
This is GridSense's master SA Reality Fit document — every later checkpoint (unit economics, financial model, capital pathway, roadmap) builds on the three local-context facts established here.

Load-shedding & infrastructure: South Africa runs on a stage-based national load-shedding system (Stage 1-8, Eskom 2024) where higher stages mean more frequent, longer outages, but the published suburb-block schedule deviates 30-90 minutes from reality in townships specifically (GridSense SA 2024 tracking, cited in CP1) because infrastructure age and localised faults aren't reflected in the national schedule. Our product design assumes intermittent, unpredictable connectivity for both the business owner's phone and any backend sync — the app must function fully offline between syncs and queue outbound SMS/data when the network itself drops during outages, which we've built as a core requirement, not an afterthought.

Data cost & device class: our real customers (CP2) run entry-level Android devices (16-32GB storage, R2,500 or under) on R50-R150/month data budgets, dominated by WhatsApp usage. This rules out any product design that assumes always-on connectivity, large background sync, or a heavy native app — GridSense is under 8MB installed and every user action (the on/off tap) costs less data than a single WhatsApp text message.

Township & income realities: our customers net R8,000-R25,000/month and currently lose R2,000-R10,000/month (CSIR 2023, cited in CP1) to diesel waste and stock spoilage from unpredictable load-shedding — this is the exact ceiling our R149/month price point must sit comfortably under to be adopted, and the exact reason our go-to-market (CP16) leans on trusted spaza-association channels rather than paid digital acquisition, which this customer segment doesn't respond to at any meaningful rate based on our 3 pilots' feedback.

priorArtifacts.name: African Scalability Logic
priorArtifacts.content:
After establishing GridSense in Gauteng and Western Cape, our next markets are Lagos, Nigeria and Nairobi, Kenya — both have well-documented grid instability affecting informal/township-equivalent SMEs, which is the precondition for our model to matter.

What changes: (1) Data baseline — Nigeria's DisCos publish far less structured outage schedules than Eskom's stage system, so our Nigeria model runs almost entirely on crowdsourced signal with no official baseline to correct, requiring a higher initial density of users per grid cell before predictions activate. Kenya's outages are more fault-driven than scheduled, so the same applies there. (2) Payment rails — Kenya's dominant channel is M-Pesa, not bank debit order like our SA billing; Nigeria needs both bank transfer and USSD-based payment support. (3) Distribution channel — Nigeria's market-trader associations and Kenya's chama/table-banking groups replace SA's spaza-shop associations as the trust-building entry point; the mechanism (partner with an existing trusted local network) stays the same, the specific network changes. (4) Language — Nigerian Pidgin/Yoruba/Hausa and Swahili localisation for SMS and app copy.

What stays the same: the core crowdsourced correction algorithm, the smart backup-power recommendation engine, the under-8MB lightweight app design for low-end devices and small data budgets, and the association-partnership go-to-market model — only the specific partner network changes per country, not the approach itself.

Real barriers: regulatory (each country needs its own local SMS-gateway/telco partnership and, in Nigeria's case, NDPR data-protection registration before launch); logistical (each new market needs an on-the-ground community manager to seed the first 3+ crowdsourced reporters per grid cell before the correction layer has any value — this is a slower, more manual cold-start than SA where Eskom's baseline schedule already gives us something useful on day one); cultural (each market's trust network takes real relationship-building time to access, not just a translated pitch deck); infrastructural (Kenya's fault-driven outage pattern means our model there needs a materially higher crowdsourced-user density before it's useful, since there's no official schedule to correct against at all — this is the single biggest expansion risk and the reason Kenya is planned after Nigeria, not simultaneously).

priorArtifacts.content:
Name: GridSense — deliberately plain English ("grid" for the power grid, "sense" for intelligent prediction), chosen because it needs to be said over the phone, in a WhatsApp voice note, or via word-of-mouth referral between spaza shop owners without translation ambiguity across the isiZulu/Sesotho/English mix common in our target townships.

Identity: positioned as a practical, no-nonsense tool for business owners, not a consumer lifestyle app — our visual identity uses a single traffic-light-style colour code (green/amber/red) for power status, deliberately matching the literacy-accessibility guidance used in SA public-health communication campaigns rather than a logo-dependent brand mark, because the trust signal that matters is instant legibility at a glance, not visual polish.

Positioning statement: "The app that knows your street's power schedule better than Eskom does." This is a specific, falsifiable claim (not "smart energy for a smarter future") and it's exactly what our pilot data (CP4) supports — 9 of 11 crowdsourced corrections matched reality where the official schedule didn't.

Defensibility against a copycat: our real moat is the crowdsourced data density itself, not the app or the algorithm, which a competitor could rebuild in weeks. A new entrant starting with zero users has zero correction accuracy — they'd need to first build the same density of trusted, active reporters per grid cell that we're building today through spaza-association partnerships, which took real relationship time to access, not just capital. This is a data-network-effect moat, not a feature moat, and it compounds the longer we operate before a copycat starts.

3-statement model summary (full model attached above, 24-month bottom-up build):

Income statement build: starting from our SOM of 7,500 reachable Gauteng/Western Cape businesses (CP3), we assume a conservative 12% penetration by month 24 (900 paying businesses) — bottom-up from our actual pilot conversion rate of 2/3 (67%) applied against a realistic association-outreach pace of 40-60 new signups/month once our CP16-funded partnerships hire is in place, not a top-down "capture 1% of TAM" guess. At R149/month ARPU, that's R134,100 MRR by month 24.

Cost build: direct costs per CP14 (SMS gateway ~R8/user/month, hosting ~R25/user/month) scale linearly with users; team costs step up in month 3 (technical co-founder hire, ~R35,000/month) and month 6 (partnerships hire, ~R28,000/month), funded by the CP16 raise.

Balance sheet: main assets are cash from the raise and accrued receivables (customers billed monthly in advance via debit order, so receivables stay near-zero); main liability is the CP16 grant/equity funding itself, held as cash until deployed against the milestone schedule in CP18.

Cash flow: burns approximately R95,000/month in months 1-6 (team ramp before revenue catches up), breaks even on a monthly cash basis around month 16 at our base-case penetration curve, giving roughly 18 months of runway on the R650,000 CP16 raise before needing a follow-on round.

Load-shedding/infrastructure cost line: we've explicitly budgeted R3,500/month for backup power and connectivity redundancy for our own small ops team, since our own operations are exposed to the same grid instability our customers face — this is a real, budgeted line item, not an oversight.

Every assumption above (penetration rate, ARPU, cost-per-user, hiring timeline) is stated with its source, per the requirement — the base case is deliberately conservative relative to our SOM ceiling from CP3, not an optimistic hockey-stick.

priorArtifacts.name: Capital Pathway
priorArtifacts.content:
We're raising R650,000, structured as a blend: R400,000 as an ESD/impact grant (targeting corporate ESD programmes and DFI-adjacent impact funds, given our majority Black-women-owned status and township-focused impact thesis) plus R250,000 as convertible equity from an angel or early-stage impact fund, rather than a single clean equity round — this reflects the reality that a pre-revenue-adjacent township SaaS venture at our stage has genuine access to South African grant capital that a pure-equity story would leave on the table.

Milestone-tied use of funds: R245,000 (month 0-6) funds a full-time technical co-founder or senior engineer hire, directly addressing the CP12 team gap and enabling us to build the automated crowdsource-density onboarding flow that currently requires manual community-manager effort. R196,000 (month 3-9) funds a dedicated partnerships/sales hire to scale past the 40-60 signups/month our founder can personally manage today, targeting the 900-paying-business milestone from CP15's base case. R119,000 (month 1-12) covers the direct cost-per-user scaling (SMS gateway, hosting) as we grow from 2 to roughly 300+ paying businesses in year one. R90,000 is held as working-capital buffer against the load-shedding-driven cost volatility flagged in CP15.

SA capital landscape fit: we're specifically targeting corporate ESD programmes with township-SME development mandates (where our beneficiary profile is a direct fit) and DFI-adjacent impact-first funds rather than traditional VC, because traditional VC's return timelines and equity expectations don't match a venture whose moat (CP9) is data-network density built over years, not a fast-scaling consumer app — we are deliberately not pitching this as a venture-scale outlier to investors who aren't the right fit for this stage and structure.

priorArtifacts.name: Moat & Risk Architecture
priorArtifacts.content:
Defensibility: our moat is the crowdsourced-correction data density itself (CP9) — a competitor can copy our app and algorithm in weeks, but they can't copy the density of trusted, active on/off reporters we've built per grid cell without repeating the same slow, relationship-based association partnerships, which took real time to access.

Honest risk catalogue:

Regulatory risk: if Eskom itself materially improves its own schedule granularity to street-level (unlikely near-term given current infrastructure, but possible over 3-5 years with smart-meter rollout), our core correction advantage narrows. Mitigation: our recommendation engine (not just the prediction) becomes the more durable value layer if this happens.

Competitive risk: EskomSePush (the incumbent consumer app) could add a business-tier product with similar crowdsourcing. They have distribution advantage but no township-SME-specific go-to-market relationships today — this is a real threat, not a hypothetical one, and our defense is moving faster into association partnerships than they're incentivised to.

Operational risk: our crowdsourcing model requires a minimum density (3+ active reporters per grid cell) to produce value — in low-density areas or early in a new market, the product simply doesn't work as well, which is a genuine cold-start weakness we haven't fully solved, only partially mitigated by leaning on Eskom's baseline schedule where crowdsourced density is thin.

Key-person risk: with only 2 team members (CP12), losing either Thandeka or Bongani in the next 6 months would materially disrupt both product development and the founder-led sales motion — this is a real and current risk, not a sanitised one, and it's the direct reason CP16's raise prioritises hiring before scaling marketing spend.

Financial risk: our LTV assumption (CP14) rests on an 18-month retention benchmark from a different company's product, not our own measured data — if our actual retention comes in materially lower, the unit economics case weakens meaningfully, and we don't have enough of our own cohort data yet to rule that out.

priorArtifacts.name: Customer Definition
priorArtifacts.content:
Our customer is a township small business owner in Gauteng and Western Cape — spaza shop owners, hair salon owners, and small manufacturers — typically aged 28-55, with roughly 55% of our current pilot customers being women-owned businesses. They run a single-room or small storefront in areas like Soweto, Diepsloot, Khayelitsha, or Delft, and net R8,000-R25,000/month, most of it reinvested into stock or equipment.

Device and data reality: they carry an entry-level Android smartphone (typically an Itel or Mobicel under R2,500, 16-32GB storage) often shared with family, with a data budget of R50-R150/month spent mostly on WhatsApp. They are wary of downloading large apps or apps that eat data in the background — this directly shapes our product decision to lead with a lightweight app plus an SMS fallback channel, not a data-heavy dashboard.

They currently rely on EskomSePush (when they have spare data) or township WhatsApp groups for load-shedding info, and either own or rent a small 2.5-5kVA generator, spending R800-R2,500/month on diesel during high-stage periods — this is the exact budget line GridSense reduces.

Township and income realities: our pricing (R149/month) is deliberately benchmarked against what they already spend guessing wrong on diesel and spoiled stock in a single bad week, not against a Silicon Valley SaaS price point — verified against the R2,000-R10,000/month loss figures from CP1's CSIR source and confirmed directly with 3 pilot customers during onboarding interviews in March 2024.

Small business owners in South African townships — spaza shop owners, hair salons, small manufacturers — lose real money every month because they can't predict exactly when load-shedding will hit their specific street, so they either run diesel generators all day just in case, or get caught without power exactly when a fridge full of stock is at risk.

Eskom's published stage schedules only give suburb-level, roughly 2-hour blocks — not a reliable start/end time for a specific street — and the active stage can change with little notice, so business owners are constantly guessing.

Documented sources (10+):
1. Stats SA (2023) Quarterly Labour Force Survey — approx. 2.3 million township-based informal/small enterprises nationally.
2. Eskom (2024) national load-shedding schedule publication — suburb-block granularity, not street-level.
3. CSIR Energy Centre (2023) report on SME economic losses from load-shedding — R2,000-R10,000/month average for stock-dependent small businesses.
4. World Bank (2023) South Africa Economic Update — load-shedding cited as the top constraint on small business growth.
5. Stellenbosch Business School (2023) survey of 500 township SMEs on load-shedding coping costs.
6. BusinessTech (2024) article on generator diesel cost inflation squeezing small business margins.
7. GridWatch SA (2024) community-reported schedule-accuracy tracking — official predictions deviate 30-90 minutes in township areas regularly.
8. Small Business Institute SA (2023) report on informal sector vulnerability to infrastructure shocks.
9. EskomSePush app store reviews (2024) — aggregated complaints about inaccurate suburb-level predictions specifically in township areas.
10. National Treasury (2023) Budget Review — notes load-shedding's disproportionate impact on informal/township economies.

Customer voice (direct):

- "I run my generator from 6am just in case, even on days there's no load-shedding at all, because I can't trust the app timing for my exact street." — Sipho, hair salon owner, Soweto (interview, March 2024).
